Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious inputs. However, in practical applications, introducing the neural network architecture to solve regression tasks results in a considerable reduction of the relevant VC dimension, thereby leading to a constraint on the bound of errors caused by malicious inputs. Moreover, as Neural ODEs feature continuous activation functions that facilitate the integration of gradient information during the optimization process, their inherent smoothness grants robustness against adversarial examples. In contrast, the inherent characteristics of Neural ODEs also enable them to withstand adversarial inputs effectively. Furthermore, our experiments using the CIFAR10 dataset demonstrate that Neural ODEs possess an impressive capacity to withstanding adversarial examples, with error rates ranging from 0% for most evaluation metrics.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through the nonlocal spatial operator $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}(t,\mathbf{x}))$ will be discussed in the context of modeling vehicular traffic. We will explore a specific free space Taylor series approximation of the nonlocal flux operator $\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{q}(t,\mathbf{x}))$ to derive a first-order approximating system of conservation laws, with a focus on its well-posedness for initial data and boundary conditions in a bounded domain. Key aspects include the emergence of a shock wave due to the nonlocal effect and the formation of a triangular region of singularities near the propagating front. We will also find conditions for the well-posedness of the approximating system and discuss how it differs from its exact counterpart. An interesting outcome of this study is the discovery that the triangular region of singularities can affect the propagation pattern of a single initial data anomaly, with a surprising result that it may not be absorbed at a boundary. In addition, the continuous dependence of solutions for boundary data and initial conditions will be investigated.

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow transition maps of varying scale within their atlases, whereas translation surfaces remain at a fixed size. This results in dilation surfaces having directional flows with unique accumulation points, known as hyperbolic closed orbits that emerge from their periodic trajectories. Research has shown that directional flows on some types of dilation surfaces, specifically those derived from slope lists, display minimal transitivity properties. Building upon this, we investigate another class of dilation surfaces, defined by a torus partitioning with a single primitive form, to better understand the intersection stability of directional flows under a specific mathematical operation that combines two dilation surfaces. This operation, known as rational surgery, is applied by translating and dilating along a torus partition. It is discovered that directional flows on surfaces with this configuration have a stable behavior under rational surgery, a finding that challenges a previously conjectured result in hyperbolic dynamics. To further explore this, we develop a procedure for determining which dilation surfaces rational surgery produces a surface with a dense flow. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of a comprehensive class of such surfaces, ensuring that a dense flow is present on a significant subset of dilation surfaces despite the initial transformation.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a method to estimate total correlation in brain network data while addressing computational limitations and noisy data. These advances enable the application of total correlation to resting-state fMRI data and allow for the investigation of its underlying mathematical characteristics. Our findings confirm the feasibility of calculating total correlation in brain network data and reveal that certain total correlation metrics can remain resilient to noise, simultaneously indicating a stronger functional connectivity between brain regions. On the other hand, some total correlation metrics prove to be more noise-sensitive or even undetermined in specific scenarios, highlighting the necessity of further statistical inference and data enhancement in such cases.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of waves and particles and the 
interplay between configuration space and phase space. This study generalizes 
those concepts to functions that use Clifford algebra. It defines unitary 
isomorphisms among spaces consisting of square-integrable Clifford algebra-valued 
functions on n-dimensional space, monogenic square-integrable functions on n+1 
dimensional space, and linear functionals on symmetric tensor elements in n 
dimensional space, each space weighted by a respective Gaussian measure.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as a universal solution for solving Bayesian posterior distributions. However, traditional techniques are impractical beyond low-dimensional problems due to inadequate efficiency. This research presents a critical evaluation of widely employed Monte Carlo methods and proposes MC2, a straightforward algorithm for approximating Gaussian process posteriors. We discuss the theoretical background, outline MC2, examine its practical applications, evaluate its effectiveness by comparing it to other methods, and highlight its practical considerations.

This research demonstrates that in outdoor settings with wireless communications employing the IEEE 802.11 protocol using dipole antennas, ground reflection is a dominant signal propagation factor. Consequently, the Two-Ray model effectively forecasts signal strength with a satisfactory degree of accuracy for this environment. Notably, the study's findings are pertinent to UAVs-over-ground sensor communication, which entails these aerial vehicles gathering information collected by ground-positioned sensors while sustaining connectivity to the base station, thereby maintaining quality of service during the process.

The last few years have seen significant advancements in the study of neutrino oscillations. Researchers have used cutting-edge experiments to measure and model the mixing and oscillation of neutrinos as they travel through different flavors. Current results from ongoing experiments are included in order to give a comprehensive review of the state of the field.

Research on top quark physics is highly effective in exploring physics that goes beyond the standard model due to the large mass of the top quark and its significant interaction with standard model particles. The second run of the LHC provided a wide range of results, and the upcoming third run will lead to the creation of a large data set. The development and use of novel variables and cuts in the examination of t t production and the mass distribution of the top quark will be heavily utilized in the LHC's future research on top quark physics. This study introduces a set of new variables that can help determine the top quark's mass in events involving two isolated leptons, numerous jets, and a large amount of hadronic transverse momentum. In comparison to established variables, the new variables led to a mass estimation that is closer to actual values in both t t+j jets and t tH production simulations. The new variables also yielded smaller uncertainties in events involving t t+j jets and both t t+j jets and t tH production.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for virtual organizations, requirement refinement, abstractions of models, and concrete instantiations. The document also examines Virtual Organizations within these contexts.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence between these strategies, we aim to clarify their common foundation, ultimately leading to the derivation of supersymmetric matrix integrals for rotation-invariant ensembles with even eigenvalue distributions.

This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning approach, known as ST-PL, that uses short observed sequences to forecast future frames and is widely applicable. One of the significant obstacles in this process is identifying long-term patterns from sequences, particularly when deep models experience degradation over time, causing their performance to significantly decline. Existing solutions mainly enhance the capabilities of deep models, although they overlook the inherent issues. In an attempt to overcome these problems, this research focuses on two related topics. Firstly, it explores the idea of representing the future in relation to the past, rather than predicting specific frames, and proposes a novel task based on this concept. Secondly, it develops a new framework for the future's inherent structural representation and proposes a complementary task to improve the model's ability to model underlying patterns. This paper demonstrates that the proposed tasks can significantly aid in addressing the issues mentioned above and provides a comprehensive framework for tackling these challenges in the field of spatiotemporal predictive learning.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for linear capabilities to enforce no-access outside data refinement on languages with tracing garbage collection, thereby making memory safety explicit for such languages. This advancement enables the integration of linear types into languages utilizing garbage collection, in turn allowing for data refinement definitions that are compatible with existing grey box verification techniques.

Theoretical particles called heavy neutral leptons have a significant role in resolving issues related to neutrino mass and light neutrino oscillation. If these particles exist, they would prevent the process of leptonic particle decay, which involves the particle decay of an electron or muon into a neutrino and a heavy neutral lepton. Research on this particle decay has become highly relevant due to the ongoing MOON and AMBER experiments. The study of particle decay in a muonic environment is particularly significant because it involves the presence of magnetic fields. We have conducted a comprehensive mathematical analysis to determine the cross section of a muon transitioning into a heavy neutral lepton accompanied by an electron or muon neutrino within a muonic environment. By considering up to four decay channels and incorporating the effects of radiation recoil, we have found that the background noise in future experiments will not hinder accurate detection of this particle decay.

Permutation decoding has become more prominent lately, allowing it to take advantage of codes' symmetries in parallel. Furthermore, research has found that by treating permuted polar codes as polar subcodes, the number of applicable permutations in permutation decoding can be enlarged. We have taken this concept a step further to pre-transformed polar codes, including those augmented with cyclic redundancy check (CRC) codes, which could see CRC-related permuted polar codes acting as cover codes to yield greater error-correction capability. Our experiments suggest that this combined technique can lead to substantial gains in permuted polar code performance.

We investigate the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. Our study centers on co-adding schemes that preserve linearity, including co-adding multiple images of the same scene captured with distinct integrations. However, we find that all linear co-adding methods have a limitation - their point spread functions become indefinitely large, resulting in ill-defined images that lack useful information. Our research also explores ways to extend the set of linear co-adding methods, allowing them to produce images with finite point spread functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all linear co-adding techniques can be generalized as convolutions with a rectangular mask, thus enabling the identification of optimal imaging strategies for producing images with specific point spread functions properties. Our findings have implications for the goals and parameters of future imaging missions, such as the Roman Space Telescope, as well as for image processing algorithms and software like astropy.stats and scipypost, by allowing us to manipulate the point spread functions of images taken by these missions and produced by these tools.

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework to explain the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic principles of phase transitions and driven by fluctuations, this model describes how dislocations emerge and spread during the fracture process. It provides a clear and unambiguous definition of the fracture toughness in terms of the fracture surface energy and the average work provided by the moving dislocations. Additionally, the formula derived for the fracture energy of a growing crack closely aligns with the findings of a renowned laboratory experiment and theoretical studies on crack behavior in metals. Furthermore, the analysis offers new insights into the underlying mechanisms of fracture that are relevant to a range of situations from common events like impact fracture to more complex phenomena such as plastic deformation in high-strain metals.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper demonstrates that the Miller-Sheffield concept can be naturally extended to the Dyson model initially studied by Mai, Rhodes, and Virag. The extension leads to the establishment of an exact relationship between the model's multiple-point fermion partition functions and Gaussian free field boundary GFFs in the context of random discrete surfaces. Furthermore, it reveals a discrete equivalent of the concept of imaginary surfaces in the context of the Dyson model.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial data, focusing on critical regularity. The outcome demonstrates analytic regularity that aligns with a conjecture from the local Navier-Stokes regularity conjecture. The proof leverages an iterative approach built on the use of the Littlewood-Paley projectors and a nondivergence form of the Navier-Stokes equations, alongside specific mathematical estimates.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a less computationally powerful classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The complexity of classical verification methods for this problem can range from polynomial time for simple cases to exponential time for more complex cases. A notable recent advancement in this area is a classical verification method for quantum circuits proposed by Hamazaki et al., which has a time complexity of nearly linear, despite requiring channel state estimation that may be computationally costly. Another significant method was introduced by Hashimoto et al. in 2021, which significantly reduces the complexity of classical verification to close to O(n^2) using standard quantum algorithms. 

In this research, we revisit the verification problem for quantum computation and develop new methods. Similar to previous work, we start by assuming the quantum server has already created a quantum state; the complexity of this step is relatively low at O(n^3/2) log(n). Our main contribution is a new, scalable method for this problem, which has a time complexity of poly(n) r^2 when the quantum circuit is factored into specific sub-circuits. 

In many practical applications of quantum computing, the verification problem can be reduced to this form with a polynomial relationship. Notably, this includes quantum chemistry calculations using the Hartree-Fock method. A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, making it a prime candidate for establishing trust within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem. However, implementing blockchain technology in the IoT setting presents significant challenges, primarily related to computational resource requirements. This problem becomes more pronounced when considering applications that demand low latency, such as event reporting. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an optimized blockchain-enabled event reporting solution for IoT, leveraging a hybrid architecture combining blockchain and radio network technologies. The proposed approach enhances event delivery reliability by utilizing distributed ledgers and implements a trustless consensus mechanism. Furthermore, the paper discusses the intricacies of applying blockchain technology to IoT and provides an experimental analysis of the proposed solution.

Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging systems. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation of a cell's geometry is necessary, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution modeling. Our proposed framework utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes, allowing for the creation of highly detailed, physiologically accurate models of neutrophil and T cell types through the use of neural networks. These SDFs, being independent of the underlying coordinate system, also facilitate model simplification and allow for the analysis of cell shapes effectively. Our synthesized cells, presented in this study, exhibit comparable morphology to actual cells according to established metrics, providing a foundation for advancing dataset creation in the field.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual analysis to identify referenced content and gather necessary summary information. An algorithm inspired by vision processing techniques is developed and tested on a large dataset to determine the effectiveness of this method.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive testing under similar settings, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across 20 tasks, including several benchmark assessments, by substantial margins.

We've developed computational models aimed at assessing the influence of stellar activity on spectroscopic analysis of exoplanet transits, particularly focusing on atmospheric characterization, by using observations of hot jupiter and hot Neptune systems. We've analyzed data from the Keck/NIRES and HST/WFC3 instruments to create reference spectra of stars with known NIRES and WFC3 spectral features. We've found that about half of the stars in our study exhibit water features on exoplanets that are strong enough to be detectable, which could potentially be masked by stellar activity. We've also simulated NIRES and WFC3 observations of 25 stars to analyze how stellar variability and activity would impact the accuracy of this detection. We've established detection limits for both stellar activity and atmospheric features, which could potentially be minimized by obtaining more observations of the same star. These findings offer a valuable tool for evaluating the feasibility of atmospheric characterization for exoplanets and informing future mission plans.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-forms. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially established by Troyanov in 1989.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this study discovered that in the presence of both air and water, this centipede primarily moves using its abdomen to create ripples while primarily moving its limb pairs on average of 6 per second which contributes to its wave like motion that aids in its gliding on the surface of water. Observations suggest the limb pairs rotate as they move, curve in an arc and squeeze to move while the study discovered the abdomen plays the major part in this movement. It was noted that waves don't develop when the centipede dives under the surface of the water; instead a form of undulation movement that resembles the wave like motion that occurs when it moves at the surface but with slower rate of movement, an increased frequency of its limb pairs and reduced amplitude of its body waves; plus when the centipede perches it merely turns its limb pairs to ensure they face downwards to aid in its rest position. It's claimed that this particular movement has yet to be discovered or studied.

This paper presents a computational model for tsunami waves that incorporates non-dispersive models into a 2D depth-dependent framework, effectively accounting for frequency-fueled dispersion in certain scenarios. Built on the approach of Taylor et al. (2007), this methodology treats buoyancy and bed friction as primary forces, formulated with laws attributed to Katsaros and Iwashita, respectively. To assess the model's performance, a comprehensive numerical analysis is carried out, covering parametric studies, an examination of idealized profiles, and the simulation of real tsunami events, including the 1958 Chilean and 1960 Kamchatka tsunamis. Further, this work addresses various engineering applications, such as the study of tsunami frequency spectra and the determination of the speed at which high-frequency waves are transmitted.

Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large, distant galaxies that are too faint to be seen in UV imaging taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. These galaxies have been referred to as HST-dark due to their elusive nature. Using high-resolution near-infrared imaging taken by the NIRCam camera, we have observed and analyzed the physical properties of this population of massive galaxies during a critical period of evolution at redshift z=4-6. Our findings reveal that these galaxies have very high star formation rates, extremely low levels of dust contamination, and compact structures. They also exhibit a wide range of stellar masses and red colors consistent with massive galaxies that have already completed their star formation. When compared to a sample of galaxies detected in UV imaging, we find that HST-dark galaxies are more massive, have been growing continuously more dense for a longer period, and have been accumulating stars at a higher rate. Our study provides new insights into the growth and evolution of massive galaxies during a major period of evolution at the onset of galaxy formation.

By incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we form a novel seven-dimensional theory of gravity. Depending on specific constant values, these terms may be equivalent to a 3-form field equation correction in eleven-dimensional supergravity. From the derived field equations, we discover new static and spherically-symmetric black holes. Interestingly, our solutions exhibit either constant or oscillating horizons. Without a negative mass gap, our findings include black holes with both zero and non-zero electric potential. Notably, we observe that the thermal phase transitions between these black holes and thermal perturbations of anti-self-dual solutions share similarities with those in duality-related D0-brane constructions in string theory.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure that the tops of the disks are closely spaced, and the flow of the disks beneath is restricted. A vast assortment of pistons with diverse properties is employed to achieve this sealing effect. This study examines the assortment of disks used in this experiment, commonly referred to as an extensible bobbin system, and focuses specifically on the arrangement of the disks when the system is in a state of mechanical equilibrium. With the exception of two theoretical models, prior studies had concluded that the disks form layers with increasing height, and then alternate between being compacted and having space, and that the distance between the top and bottom pistons fluctuates unpredictably. In contrast, we present a simple method for precisely calculating the appearance of the disks when the system is in a state of mechanical equilibrium. This approach takes into account the movement of the pistons and the arrangement within the disks, and it does so by identifying the optimal configuration of the disks, and then determining the range of the disks' mechanical properties within which the system remains stable. It also examines an associated statistical mechanics problem.

El Niño events exhibit varying patterns of precipitation around the globe. The East Pacific and Central Pacific types of El Niño have distinct effects on atmospheric and oceanic conditions in the Eastern Pacific, leading to distinct relationships between El Niño events and the presence of clouds, precipitation, and wind patterns. The East Pacific type of El Niño tends to extend into the Amazon rainforest, impacting its water balance and causing drought that could potentially threaten the forest's integrity. Contrasting this, the Central Pacific type of El Niño brings precipitation to the Pacific Islands, reducing the risk of drought in the region.

When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to mechanical pressure, the distortion they undergo may deviate from expected behavior, even within their elastic range. The extent of nonaffine behavior, a concept observed in various numerical models, poses a significant challenge to experimental studies due to its low-scale deformation. A new approach has been developed that combines infrared spectroscopy and atomic force microscopy to analyze this nonaffine contribution within model materials consisting of glass particles and polymers. The use of two techniques - contact and near-contact - has been shown to enable measurement of the nonaffine modulus, even at low temperatures. A nonaffine prediction model has been created to analyze the material's behavior across its entire elastic range, providing insights into its mechanical properties. The availability of this multi-scale, room-temperature method may facilitate further studies on materials that behave in this manner.

This research investigates a population model, factoring in the effects of age and environmental pollution, comprising a single population with distinct larval and adult stages. The model uses logistic functions, and larvae are converted into adults at a constant rate, focusing solely on adult development. The study incorporates psychological impacts by representing adult-environment interactions with a functional relationship and larvae-environment interactions with a linear one.

To determine the stable states of this model, presented as invariant sets where it's stable or unstable, the Lyapunov function method is applied. The results show that the model exhibits a single, indeterminate fixed point, depending on parameter values, and that adult-environment interactions influence its stability. The study concludes by highlighting the significance of considering both age and environmental factors in population models, especially regarding the single fixed point's sensitivity to parameter values and environmental factors.

The researchers achieve a significant breakthrough by making the consequences of weakening propositional aspects of commutative Full Lambek logic soluble. 
This achievement builds upon an earlier result showing cutting axioms from a smaller, symmetric variant of the logic, which the authors further developed by making the logic's cut-free calculation formula modular using biordered sets. 
As a result of this breakthrough, it is also proven that certain aspects of the linear logic lambek$\rightarrow_{L} ; \rightarrow_{R}$ are decidability established.

Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research has sought to automatically enhance existing taxonomies by learning concept representations in Euclidean space. However, the natural geometric structure of taxonomies aligns better with hyperbolic properties, making this space more suitable for representation. We propose HyperExpan, an algorithm that preserves the hierarchical structure of a taxonomy within a more expressive hyperbolic embedding space. It employs graph neural networks to capture relationships and characterizes profile information of concepts for accurate prediction during hyperparameter tuning. Evaluations on various benchmarks confirm that HyperExpan outperforms models operating in Euclidean space and achieves state-of-the-art results within hyperbolic space.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate hydrogen bonding associated with a binary mixture of acetone and water in the context of strong electric fields. Effective pair potential models have been created for the two systems, allowing the variation of water and acetone to be accurately simulated. Furthermore, ab initio and ab initio-based molecular dynamics studies have demonstrated that the orientation of molecules in electric fields leads to substantial dipole moments. These observations are consistent across various scenarios, including situations where water and acetone are in excess, under excess-solute conditions, and at different field intensities up to a magnitude of 2 V/(r0) of approximately 1 V/(r0) cm. Notably, the orientation of molecules in electric fields is more pronounced when water acts as a hydrogen bond donor or acceptor and is primarily responsible for the phenomenon's onset. Analysis of energy profiles reveals that the system's energy exhibits maximal deviation at field intensities of approximately 1.5 V/(r0) of approximately 0.7 eV. These observations are consistent with MD simulations conducted under excess-solute conditions, which reveal system energies that deviate by up to 1.5 eV as a result of orientation. Additionally, the effectiveness of pair potential in capturing energy data is validated, with the exception of situations characterized by high field intensities of approximately 2 V/(r0) of approximately 1 eV. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and efficiency, incorporating data analytics and cyber-physical systems for enhanced planning and scheduling. Nonetheless, uncertainties inherent in environmental factors and operator subjectivity often go unaccounted for in decision-making, causing shipment delays and inaccuracies in budget projections. This widespread issue demands correction, and existing approaches have explored solutions via stochastic or fuzzy logic models. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for quantifying non-deterministic uncertainty through probabilistic modeling, which is universally applicable to various industrial datasets. A practical case study demonstrates the efficacy of this method by infusing real-world data into an existing scheduling system for performance improvement.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. We provide a measurable Resilience Satisfaction Value, which evaluates resiliency on a scale, considering two key factors: swift recovery from disturbances and sustained stability. The practicality of our approach is demonstrated through the use of case studies, marking a breakthrough in understanding multi-dimensional resiliency semantics, whereas previous formulations merely target swift recovery.

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based research particularly intriguing. This research explores the potential of accelerometers as dark matter detectors, particularly in relation to axions, scalar fields, and scalar particles. To achieve this, we simulate an accelerometer in a state-of-the-art laboratory environment and replicate the conditions of currently operating dark matter experiments, such as LUX-Zeplin and XENON1T, using laboratory-specific constraints on axion and scalar interactions. Our results suggest that accelerometers can rival the sensitivity of these prestigious dark matter experiments under specific laboratory conditions.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which have a positive, smooth, and bounded u. The equation u_t is given by \[ \Delta u - \nabla \phi \cdot \nabla u = (au + b) \log u. \] In our analysis, a and b are positive constants, with \phi being a smooth function on the manifold. Our findings extend existing work in the literature, including a prior investigation involving Euclidean space.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to Galactic magnetic fields affects larger sources. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having an inaccessible internal process, allowing for predictions to be made based on observable symptoms, while the internal workings remain hidden. Although HMMs have been found useful in various applications such as speech and medical diagnostics, training an HMM using labeled data can be an unsupervised task, but typically requires an additional step of model adjustment using unsupervised validation methods. The main issue arises when dealing with large data sets containing thousands of sequences, but with limited annotation available only at the sequence level. The training of HMMs in such scenarios often results in poorly performing models due to the complexity of the problem. The proposed Solution Training HMM with an Ensemble of Entropy-based Selection of Hidden States (STERES) aims to address this issue through an innovative approach. TheSTERES method trains an HMM by first developing multiple versions of the model, which are generated by applying an entropy-based method to determine the most complex parameters. TheSTERes method then uses an enhanced version of the Baum-Welch algorithm to optimize the parameters of the individual models combined. The approach effectively prevents the overfitting of the models to the limited available data. The proposed method outperformed traditional approaches by providing better performance on the dataset for an HMM-based task. We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity, with the turbulent intensity being the associated diffusion coefficient. However, in scenarios where non-locality plays a dominant role, the conventional estimate fails, leading to an inherent error. We demonstrate that in the intra-cone region of the Taylor micro-scale, the turbulent transport operator can be represented by the sum of a standard hyperdiffusivity operator and its complement, which describes non-local turbulent transport. A corresponding sub-filter model is proposed and validated by comparing it with direct numerical simulation data from various Taylor micro-scale regimes.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
lacking a complete understanding of the dynamics behind nucleon-nucleus and
nucleus-nucleus scattering. When phenomenological models are too limited,
vital information about the processes is lost. We advocate an alternative
phenomenology for nuclear elastic scattering involving nucleons and light nuclei,
which effectively evaluates folding models and leverages available empirical
evidence related to the underlying physical interactions. This approach was
applied to the $^6$Li + $^{48}$Ti$^{4}$ scattering system, analyzed within a
$n + \alpha + n + N$ correlation model that successfully accounts for the full
range of observed data. Key aspects, such as the angular distribution at
backscatter and characteristics of the quasielastic and inelastic processes,
coincide with experimental findings, supporting this comprehensive understanding of
the $^6$Li + $^{48}$Ti system.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation behavior in a thin conductor plate separated by two large parallel walls at a temperature $T$, where the plate's area is $A$ and the distance between the walls is $d$. We utilize $T$, $A$, and $d$ as primary parameters to calculate the electromagnetic radiation's thermodynamic properties. It is observed that a non-extensive Caldirola-Cannone calculus leads to a modified Caldirola-Cannone-Langevin equation, which includes a temperature-dependent time scale ($\tau = \frac{m\gamma_0 T}{e}$) in the coherent state. We derive the probability density and coherent energy of the system using this new time scale. Subsequently, the free energy, its thermodynamic behavior, and dissipative properties are investigated. Notably, the system exhibits anomalous thermodynamic behavior at low temperatures, where entropy increases with temperature, refuting Kelvin's and Planck's statements. Additionally, irreversible processes are inherent in the system even in the absence of dissipation mechanisms.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary.

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling large-scale point cloud matching at high speeds with the combination of the nlists data structure, the transformer model, and the 2D-3D point registration method. The notable benefits of this method include the use of query-key attention for point reconstruction, as well as the incorporation of token-level response outputs in point cloud mapping. Evaluations using the CoNavTech dataset demonstrated NDT-Transformer's exceptional performance, outperforming existing approaches by means of both precision and recall metrics. Notably, this method is expected to achieve an 80% accuracy rating of precise matches in the CoNavTech dataset when system response times do not exceed 300 milliseconds.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes, mainly affecting our ability to identify individual differences. We observed that adapting a model that accounts for site-to-site effects can significantly enhance our ability to detect group differences. Therefore, our results provide crucial guidance for designing future multisite resting-state functional MRI studies.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to achieve the most efficient solution with optimal run times and minimal station memory. For the naming problem, we present a new, optimized algorithm enabling each station to determine its unique identifier as close as possible to the square root of the total number of stations. Meanwhile, the counting problem can be resolved in approximately the same timeframe, allowing each station to estimate the total number of stations with an accuracy of at least half of the square root of the total number of stations, given that every station can hear all other stations. These algorithms use a minimal amount of station memory, necessitating only two registers, and they function efficiently even when the presence of a adversary affects the communication process. These solutions improve previous algorithms by significantly shortening the naming algorithm's run time to be close to the square root of n (formerly $\sqrt{n\log n}$) and reducing the counting issue from $n\log n$ to approximately the square root of n.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained substantial attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
like n-gram models fail to capture the inherent context of language switching, 
while purely neural networks sometimes produce sub-optimal results due to their 
global optimization of loss functions without considering switching points. 
This study investigates the effectiveness of utilizing additional network components 
for modulating the context of language switching and introduces a novel module 
called the Language Switching Module, integrated within the Word2Vec framework, 
which excels at building code-mixed language word embeddings compared to state-of- 
the-art baseline models.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experiments, particularly at high pressures, suggesting the importance of its van Hove singularities in superconducting H3S compounds.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are often unsuccessful without pre-compiled maps or where environmental maps become obsolete due to sudden changes like traffic congestion, roadblocks, or construction. Triangulation-based methods are viable alternatives but have limitations in dynamic environments. In an effort to improve upon this, we have devised a novel method using a sequence of spatial channels that accommodate multiple triangulation structures, serving as spatial boundaries for navigation in unstructured environments. Our approach is tested and compared with other triangulation-based methods on a drone navigation task within the 'Berkeley Drone Dataset'.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine 6-DoF camera poses by leveraging the constructed visual database. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions. Our approach is demonstrated to achieve high accuracy under both real-world and simulated scenarios.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves a particular semifield defined as the set of real numbers with maximum and addition, and also a particular subsemifield defined as the set of numbers greater than or equal to 1 with maximum and multiplication, and that it is isomorphic to the semifield of finite rational functions on a particular type of curve called an extended ray. Furthermore, an isomorphism exists between this semifield and the semifield of finite rational functions on another particular type of curve called a tropical ray.

This study focuses on the asymptotic behavior of discrete-time Markov processes under specific conditions. A preliminary assumption is made regarding a quasi-stationary distribution, which remains stationary within a particular subset under the processes' limiting distribution. Based on this premise, both local and global decay or persistence criteria are developed, building upon initial work by Donsker and Khas'movsky. Specifically, we derive local limit theorems and laws of iterated logarithm limits for Markov chains, as well as persistent phenomena, by examining critical factors such as spatial and temporal characteristics. A distinct feature of our work involves examining Markov processes in continuous spaces, as opposed to those in finite or discrete spaces, as addressed in earlier research by Donsker and Khas'movsky (1978) and Donsker (1986).

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the same researchers, which stated that I(X) integrated over the Gramain-Morlet 1-cycles generates the standard invariant, delta chi, of a long knot, known to be an invariant of order two. Investigators are now motivated to delve into the realm of closed one-dimensional manifolds to explore how the integrations of 1-cycles over various spaces of a long knot yield distinct Vassiliev invariants of varying orders.

The connection between superconducting and antiferromagnetic phases in iron-based superconductors continues to be a topic of interest. The phase diagram of LiFeAs, a well-known iron-based superconductor below 10 K, has been explored using resistivity, specific heat, and muon spin rotation relaxation and diffusion measurements. These measurements reveal that both the superconducting and antiferromagnetic phases undergo a second-order phase transition with exponential temperature depolarization rates, suggesting the continuity of their respective order parameters. However, by analyzing the temperature dependence of the exponential rates, it can be determined whether the superconducting and antiferromagnetic order parameters are identical. In this study, the temperature dependence of the exponential rates shows that the superconducting and antiferromagnetic order parameters exhibit distinct temperature variations. Consequently, the observed continuity of the phase transitions does not necessarily imply that the same physical mechanism is driving both phases. Instead, it can be attributed to the inherent material properties of LiFeAs. Furthermore, the study also reveals that the superconducting phase can survive in the absence of the antiferromagnetic phase due to the significantly smaller strength of the ferromagnetic correlations in LiFeAs. Additionally, the research finds that the ferromagnetic correlations in this material are predominantly controlled by the spin dynamics rather than being driven by electron dynamics. Furthermore, the study provides an estimate for a critical magnetic field of approximately 8 tesla for rotating magnetic moments in LiFeAs

This research reviews a global analysis of Type-II two Higgs doublet models and considers how upcoming measurements of the SM-like Higgs and Z-pole may influence allowed model parameters. Based on a global analysis of two Higgs doublet models using the GAMBIT tool, our study takes into account numerous current constraints, including theoretical requirements, experimental search results, and physical constraints on flavour. Furthermore, we evaluate whether forthcoming facilities, like the High-Luminosity LHC, the Circular Electron Positron Collider, the International Linear Collider, and the Future Circular Collider, electron edition will be capable of probing two Higgs doublet model parameters.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles and temporal strategies for enhancing spontaneous assembly processes, based solely on the desired properties of the final product and the properties of available building blocks, not requiring any prior understanding of the assembly outcome. This overcomes the limitations of current surface-dressing techniques that heavily depend on prior scientific knowledge about the system. Furthermore, this design can produce not only static structures but also dynamic materials with specific temporal responses that can be controlled by external stimuli, such as temperature or application of a static or oscillating electric field.

Our research appears to suggest a dynamical-Higgs-phase outcome in a broad range of chiral gauge theories, particularly those that are strongly-coupled. In contrast, a different scenario featuring flavor symmetric vacuums with massless baryonlike composite fermions does not seem as likely. The possibility of formulating a strong-anomaly effective action, similar to one applied to QCD, using the infrared theory's low-energy degrees of freedom serves as a key criterion in our argument. Additionally, our findings also pertain to other theories that are closely related, such as the large-$N$ unitarity limit of chiral gauge theories and the quiver-type formulations that pertain to strongly-coupled gauge theories.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between input forces and resulting flows in dimension d. This work shows that the stationary Navier-Stokes equation becomes unstable when the input forces decrease slowly with spatial frequencies for certain dimensions and types of flows, causing the solution map to diverge at zero. Conversely, we find that this divergence is not a concern when the input forces decrease rapidly, and we specifically identify cases where this is true for 3D and 4D systems. These findings are facilitated by novel analyses that challenge previous assumptions and have been shown to be incorrect, and they also address the relationship between these results and the theories of turbulence and hydrodynamic stability.

We are studying how the interactions between magnons in collinear antiferromagnetic crystals affect the polarization of the modes and their ability to be polarized when an external magnetic field is applied. By applying a technique based on the polarization of the real axis, we have developed a method to calculate how the interactions affect the polarization of the modes. This method works for any type of magnetic crystal when the applied field is not too strong, and it can also be used to study how the polarization changes when the applied field gets stronger. To demonstrate its use, we have used the interaction parameters obtained from a well-known type of magnetic crystal to show how the polarization of the modes changes as the applied field gets stronger.

This research introduces two security enhancements for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem:
1. Employing a vector form of the Reed-Malus code instead of the group variant.
2. Utilizing the rank-based McEliece decryption procedure. Both of these modifications are theoretically founded and offer guaranteed security benefits. Furthermore, we examine the computational efficiency of our method using the Gilbora code and compare it with Loidreau's system based on the group variant of the Reed-Malus code in terms of public key size and decryption complexity. It's discovered that the vector form yields significantly smaller public keys and faster decryption times, especially for larger code lengths.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new ways
to enhance model performance. The quality of these word meanings depends on how
often the words appear in the data, leading to underoptimized representations of
infrequent words. This paper investigates a novel method to address this issue by
leveraging dictionaries like Wiktionary to define rare words. The rare word's
definition is added to the input text, along with two novel tasks: word and
sentence alignment. This enhanced model, Dict-BERT, is evaluated on various NLP
benchmarks and shows significant improvement in processing rare words and
overall performance on NLP tasks.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. A recent study of these structures focused on the expected weight convergence. In this work, we investigate the distribution of weights of a minimum spanning acycle when only partial data is available. Our findings include that the empirical distribution of acycle weights is connected to the structure that results when replacing weights on faces with ones, and that this distribution does not change as additional weights are added. Furthermore, the calculated expectations match previous results. From a practical standpoint, our findings open up possibilities for the study of minimum weight structures in terms of probability measures.

In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables multiple entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two main types - horizontal and vertical FL. The text focuses on implementation details for horizontal FL, presented as a set of guidelines that combine Python and FL libraries, including PySygma, TensorFlow, and PyTorch. The goal is to guide readers on integrating FL into applied projects, enhancing data privacy.

A theoretical framework called B-Mesogenesis, which involves the decay of B mesons into proton-like particles, is analyzed by examining three-time correlation events of the type $pp\bar{pp\bar{p}}$. Data from the Belle II experiment at the Super B Factory in Japan, based on a dataset expected to be 50 times larger than the original, could potentially reveal B-mesons decaying into baryons and it's hypothesized that this discovery could be made before the completion of the experiment.
