A detailed likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model in order to assess its ability to explain observed anomalies in rare decays of $B$ mesons, particularly the anomalies associated with $b\to c l \overline{\nu}$ and $b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ transitions. This analysis finds that the model effectively addresses the anomalies associated with $b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ transitions and is also capable of explaining data related to $B^{(}\overrightarrow{0})\rightarrow K^{(\ast)}\bar{\tau}\tau$ and $B_{q}\rightarrow K^{(\ast)\tau^{\overrightarrow{+}}\tau^{-}}$. Furthermore, in light of the anomalies associated with $b\to c l \overline{\nu}$ transitions, it appears that the parameter space for the two Higgs doublet model is somewhat restricted, although it still aligns well with its off-shell contribution to the $W$ mass and the observed masses and mixings of the Higgs boson, as reported by the PT/SYMC collaboration. Finally, in a related lepton flavor universality test, it has been found that the two Higgs doublet model is capable of explaining data related to $R(D^{(}\overrightarrow{0})$ and $D_{s}^{(\ast))}$, although this result is somewhat tentative, as it

This study introduces a unique, self-contained three-dimensional random vortex system that mirrors the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations for non-viscous incompressible fluid flows. The newly developed random vortex system incorporates a stochastic differential equation that interacts with a finite-dimensional system of differential equations, influencing the distribution of vorticity (Q). By demonstrating the existence and unicity of the solution to this system, the research further establishes that the duality of the conditional distribution of the vorticity (Q(-t)|_0) with respect to a Brownian motion and a deterministic system of equations creates a form of Donsker's theorem. This result has implications for understanding the convergence properties in nonlinear fluid dynamics.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using S single photons passed through beam splitters with M modes, facilitating a description of its initial state using generalized coherent states. Due to its polynomial scaling with M, it is now possible to study Renyi entanglement entropies for systems containing large numbers of modes and moderate numbers of particles. Our findings include the existence of Renyi index-independent, symmetric Page curves, where maximum entropy occurs when the top N eigenvalues of the reduced system density matrix are equally distributed. In contrast to pure systems, this occurs at N less than half the total particle number. Additionally, it is observed that the entanglement rate increases logarithmically with M, prior to reaching the maximum entropy point, before slowing down to linear growth beyond this point, similar to the von Neumann entropy for pure states.

Temporal sequences in various disciplines like molecular dynamics, climate trends, and economic patterns, require analysis over extended periods. Current time-series analysis techniques are inefficient, even simplified financial data needing weeks to months for computation and maintenance. To streamline this process, a new method, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, has been developed. It efficiently maps large sequences onto one-dimensional space, preserving key information, and doing so in a matter of seconds. By incorporating artificial neural networks and focusing on crucial details, SGTM-TT successfully identifies critical events and maintains precise relationships between these events and their corresponding sequence values. In comprehensive tests across multiple disciplines, SGTM-TT outperformed existing methods, and its potential to significantly reduce exploration time by up to 100 times was demonstrated. By efficiently visualizing this reduced data, SGTM-TT facilitates the discovery of hidden patterns in temporal sequences.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events and previous actions. Recent research utilizes deep neural networks to store and process this sequence information to improve the approximation of valuation functions. We propose a new algorithm to further enhance valuation function approximation by training a network to focus on the most relevant sequence details for these functions. This detection is based on a new, optimized method for representing and identifying repeated patterns in sequences. We find that our algorithm is effective in identifying critical pattern elements and improving the approximation of valuation functions, ultimately yielding better returns for agents.

In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks. However, we believe that understanding an action involves also considering its context - objects and individuals within a video scene - so we've developed a novel model integrating self-attention and graph convolutional networks to better model context dependencies. Our approach tackles a unique set of challenges including identifying relevant objects and individuals within a video sequence, tracking their movements over time, and aggregating features for final classification. We test our method on a recently introduced dataset featuring long-action videos of people interacting in 3D environments, demonstrating state-of-the-art precision and context awareness when identifying action start and end points.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping of images, incorporation into unrelated content, combined with pixel-level disturbances. Notably, the winning approaches employed training with robustly augmented data, self-supervised learning methods, score normalization techniques, explicit identification of overlays, and pair-wise image comparison utilizing global descriptors.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, along with a smaller, non-degenerate perturbation. Since the pioneering work of Stroock and Stroock in 1991, a rigorous approach has been employed to establish a reflection principle for these types of processes. Despite significant advancements in this field, a key challenge remains unsolved: proving that the metastable behavior of these processes remains valid even as the magnitude of the perturbation approaches zero. In this paper, we address this challenge head-on by providing a comprehensive proof for a broad class of stochastic processes that operate in a specific mathematical framework known as Gromov. Our research also involves generalizing our findings to any dimensionality and further expands our metastability analysis to a broad range of interfaces that are not necessarily one-dimensional, while still maintaining our initial assumptions about the process' behavior. Additionally, we present a conceptually distinct approach that simplifies the analysis of these processes in the context of growing interfaces.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetric function in relation to the spin polarization parameter. As a result, our calculations indicate that very strong magnetic fields can significantly influence the properties of nuclear matter, shifting the energy minimization point in relation to the spin polarization parameter. Furthermore, our calculations of the spin polarization parameter at the energy minimization point, as well as the compression modulus, display an oscillating behavior in response to magnetic field intensity and nuclear density variations.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at two distinct wavelengths. The UV intensity in the area exhibited significant variation, with diffuse UV radiation largely resulting from dust particles scattering starlight. By analyzing the albedo spectrum, the study identified eight distinct groups based on the apparent stars in the region and determined that red dwarf stars up to 10th magnitude were the dominant source of scattered UV radiation. It further estimated that 20-40% of UV radiation in this area came from the central stars of dark clouds, and also detected four ALFALFA galaxies whose starlight contributed to the UV emission. The calculated dust-to-gas ratio in the region varied between 120-140 and correlated well with CO intensity, thus validating the validity of dust-based gas density calculation in this case. Moreover, it has been observed that gas in this region is largely neutral rather than ionized, with ionized gas largely existing in filaments. The study also found a 40% correlation between neutral gas and visual extinction, which suggested that dust in this region is largely three-dimensional. It has also been observed that UV radiation in this region has a tendency to exist in filaments rather than in molecular clouds.

Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, retaining readability and making it easier to grasp concepts, regardless of whether they're presented in research papers, textbooks, or conference submissions. Due to the widespread availability of document images, there's a significant need to accurately extract tables and transform them into machine-readable formats. This paper introduces a novel, real-time table detection and extraction system that utilizes an optimized, efficient procedure. This method encompasses two primary components: a deep learning model based on YOLO that locates the table boundaries, and a subsequent module that interprets the detected boundaries to extract the table correctly. Through extensive testing with various document datasets, we demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems in terms of speed and achieves superior results in extracting tables accurately.

This study undertakes a comprehensive examination of the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory in the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. Starting from a foundational theory, it presents a framework for evaluating the cognitive abilities of players along a hierarchical spectrum. These agents seek to maximize their own utility and recognize that more refined players than themselves possess superior strategic insight. The paper develops a method for quantifying the cognitive level of players through their examination of opponent strategies, resulting in a proposed agent profile. It demonstrates that the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory can generate a stable equilibrium with bounded cognitive levels. Furthermore, the study provides insight into the cognitive characteristics required for such equilibrium points. Notably, it highlights instances where agents necessitate an increase in cognitive level over time and explores the circumstances leading to infinite cognitive escalation. The research also explores a scenario where agents have varied hierarchical levels and demonstrates that some players may experience changes in their cognitive level as a continuous process, while others require discrete increments.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. We conducted an experiment in Mozambique, specifically estimating the population count in two districts between censuses. Furthermore, we evaluated the feasibility of leveraging open-access datasets to support population forecasting. Our exploration also involved utilizing existing annotated datasets to improve building footprint prediction, coupled with additional annotation of 'dot' features from targeted areas to enhance accuracy. We found that population estimates improved when utilizing building footprint estimates derived from annotated datasets over those with unannotated features.

Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. Moreover, adaptive solutions have recently been introduced, enabling the avoidance of potential errors in data queries for specific elements. This research aims to introduce a new type of static filter that eliminates incorrect positive results for negative data sets, thereby reducing false positives. Unlike existing solutions, the proposed filter utilizes a distinct structure from xor filters and can also eliminate negative false positives using a straightforward recovery approach. Furthermore, the occurrence of incorrect negative results in this structure can be minimized through post-processing. Experimental findings show that the proposed filter in both xor and xor- filter scenarios outperforms existing solutions in terms of storage efficiency while maintaining comparable or lower false positive rates. Finally, the occurrence of incorrect negative results in this structure is shown to have a straightforward relationship with the expected data size, thereby enabling the estimation of false negatives using statistical analysis, thereby making it easier to determine when a further decrease in false negatives would result in a significant improvement in system efficiency.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements.

The previous SPH method had some drawbacks when applied to multi-physics coupled problems such as fluid-structure interactions. To address these limitations, a high-performance multi-resolution SPH framework has been developed to efficiently solve FSI problems. This approach integrates mathematical tools for fluid and solid continuum equations, a weak formulation for parallel processing, and several SPH innovations. A novel local optimization technique for multi-physics coupled equations, a multi-domain optimization method, and multi-domain kinematic relationships are also introduced. Furthermore, a hierarchical data structure is utilized to accelerate computations. Numerical simulations of Riesz vortex, airfoil motion at sub-reynolds numbers, and heart disease models demonstrate the potential of this new framework in medical simulations. Its robustness is proven in various FSI problems, including an artificial heart model. This SPH framework combines accuracy, computational efficiency, and performance, enabling reliable multi-physics simulations.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets has become essential to daily life. Traditional machine learning methods, however, are limited by the data processing constraints of conventional computing. This is where quantum computing excels, enabling the efficient handling of large datasets and rapid adaptation to complex systems through unitary operations. This review focuses on the latest developments in quantum-assisted machine learning, covering topics such as quantum neural networks, quantum algorithms, and related research progress in China. It also discusses ongoing challenges and the potential applications of these approaches to solving pressing global issues, such as healthcare and environmental concerns, and predicts that these quantum algorithms may experience significant advancements in the next 10-20 years, ultimately leading to their widespread adoption in industry applications.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two ways to fix this issue.  First, we changed the model to make changing the pitch less sensitive to it, which lets FastPitch speak in a wider range of pitches.  Second, we developed a pitch-shifting algorithm that doesn't change the sound of the speaker's voice, which helps the quality of the speech made with it.  We compared these methods to FastPitch in a speech test and found that the speech test results showed the improvement.

This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video, even when they interact with other objects and undergo visual transformations. Traditional videoswitch models, including those applying transformer structures, have generated outstanding results for task-based methods, but have primarily focused on achieving accurate predictions rather than identifying the specific steps involved in their decision-making processes. We establish the Video Object Transformation Model, a novel neural architecture built upon transformer structures that incorporates explicit object tracking and transformation mechanisms. This model makes predictions at individual frame-levels while simultaneously optimizing an inverse video prediction loss, leveraging the output of a separate detector to identify objects and their transformations in video frames. We use a joint learning strategy that combines the detector and transformer outputs to refine the model's object tracking capabilities. We develop comprehensive tests for object-based video reasoning with a focus on object permanence and integration into a comprehensive video understanding framework. Our approach excels in performance on this specific task, surpassing top-performing methods as well as methods integrated into more complex pre-trained vision models.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The calculations take into account all the key aspects involved, including detailed simulations of bottom quark origin and the effects of additional radiation. The results derived can be applied in various stages of the collider's operation. Additionally, we compare these predictions to data from the 2016 LHC measurement. In a separate development, we derive a simplified model describing how the production of these lepton pairs pairs is influenced by the relevant underlying processes at the LHC, specifically when one or both of the initial particles are not fully proton-based. The focus of our model is on the scenario where the bottom quark originates from one of the partons. The derived model is useful in analyzing the relevant underlying processes at the LHC that contribute to neutral-current Drell-Yan production.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. A crucial factor for these robots' acceptance is ensuring users have a satisfying experience while interacting remotely, including effortless navigation. This research focuses on an overlooked aspect of remote control: the navigation aspect. An extensive study evaluated the Quality of Experience (QoE) for using Telepresence robots via the internet by impairing the participants' network connection, making their experience more challenging in terms of visual and navigation control. The results show that users can easily distinguish between their visual and navigation capabilities, and their experience sensitivity varies based on the specific task being performed.

In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full probabilistic frameworks, including the conditional distributions for each parameter. We extend these models to incorporate a linear relationship between the second-stage mean and a set of relevant predictor variables. The implementation details of the employed Gibbs sampling algorithms are thoroughly described, which are essential for generating samples when estimating model parameters. Furthermore, a real-world example examines the effect of nitrogen soil concentration and a categorical variable (farm) on plant size.

The game "Mafia," also known as "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to be taken, with lynching occurring during the day phase. Mafia members possess special abilities that distinguish them from the citizens, who are the dominant group due to their higher numbers. Researchers have developed a mathematical model that reflects the game's dynamics through a probability distribution, known as the "phase distribution," which describes the likelihoods of each phase having been reached in the game's progression. A previous study by these authors focused on the early stages of the game's progression and derived specific mathematical outcomes, including the inverse square root proportion of mafia members versus citizens, which is also observed in the game's early night phases. Additionally, a mathematical limit of the phase distribution's variance was established in the game's advanced stages. Both of these outcomes are rooted in the fundamental differences between the mafia and citizen groups.

Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected by the dynamics of their protoplanetary
disks. We used long-term simulations to study the development of planetary
accretion and its impact on systems with two planets, starting from identical
planet seeds that form within the disks around solar-mass stars. The simulations
revealed that planetary mass acquisition is determined by the position of the
planets in relation to the inner edge of the disk, caused by the insides of the
disks heating up. In systems where one planet is closer to the star than the other,
the inner planet finishes forming first and starts to influence its sibling's mass
gain. Alternatively, in systems where the inner planet is farther from the star,
the outer planet's mass growth is delayed, giving the inner planet an extended
period of time to influence the outer planet's mass gain. In both scenarios, the
mass ratio of the planets is influenced by when mass accumulation occurs, with
systems that form later in their lifetimes producing planets with a wider mass
difference between their giant planets compared to systems that form earlier in
their lifetimes. These results are consistent with observations of planetary
systems with varying mass ratios for their giant planets, indicating that these
planets may have formed within a protoplanetary disk that is dynamic and
undergoes changes over time.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on vibrational modes within the materials, as these phonons interact with
each other and influence electrical transport. A theory has been developed to measure
lateral heat transfer in graphene properties using Raman spectroscopy, as a non-
destructive method that provides insights into the materials' structure. Two-dimensional
materials exhibit unique heat conduction properties, and their mass per unit length
affect heat movement across the materials. The graphene properties can be analyzed
by examining the width of a second-order Raman signal. A calibration process is used
to measure heat conductivity in specific directions of the materials. An equation has
been devised to determine the ratio of a particular material's properties as they
relate to their size and the stiffness of their molecular structure. A new method has
been developed to measure flexibility in individual carbon nanotubes using a unique
optical technique that utilizes near-field light. A certain model has been developed to
estimate a particular value related to the materials' flexibility in carbon nanotubes. 
Carbon nanotubes properties can be analyzed by measuring curvature in the materials
through their flexibility values.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach tailored for clustering high-dimensional data in mixed environments. The algorithm is specifically designed for datasets with imbalanced features where some attributes are more significant than others. Differing from conventional fuzzy k-means, our method incorporates weight adjustments based on the entropy of cluster memberships for improved partitioning. Evaluations on simulated and actual data sets demonstrate the superior performance of our approach. Notably, our results show that the performance of our algorithm surpasses that of the standard fuzzy k-means and the State-of-the-art FSKM-AE approach on both simulated and actual data sets.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear expert functions. In contrast to existing methods, this new approach relies on a unique weight update rule for experts that is straightforward, conceptually simple, and free from intricate mathematical calculations. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that our approach converges to an optimal solution within a single iteration and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms across multiple evaluation criteria by achieving lower training and testing error rates.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence in both Particle Physics and Cosmology theories suggests that globally symmetric islands could exist within microphysical models, enabling a deeper understanding of fundamental laws. Discovering potentially globally static gravitational waves could confirm these hypotheses. We propose a comprehensive model of an isolated, static universe that is consistent with quantum gravity and features globally restored $U(1)$ symmetry. In this model, a massive, spinning universe contains naturally occurring globally static gravitational waves that are pure quantum states. Specifically, these waves are formed from spin-2 gravitational fields that emulated monopole modes of a cosmic 2-sphere and are characterized by minimal perturbations of the universe's spin. Notably, the model's form factors accelerate the decay of the universe's massive state from a quantum perspective, with decay rates proportionally increasing with the mass and decreasing with the radius. Conversely, the model's form factors decelerate decay via quantum tunneling. Moreover, the model describes an extremely long-lived universe with a large radius relative to its mass, consistent with the de Sitter model's asymptotic state and the model's form factors again accelerating and tunneling as factors. In this model, the universe's mass determines the temperature scale, with mass and temperature having an inversely proportional relationship. Notably, the model describes a quantum state for the universe with an infinitely high temperature.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the source's cluster membership using Gaia data. Our FUV-optical analyses allowed for the identification of UV-bright stars which could be categorized into three distinct populations: blue horizontal branch stars, blue straggler stars, and white dwarfs. Furthermore, first-ever far ultraviolet to red optical spectroscopic observations of 10 UV-bright stars yielded radial velocities which aligned with those of the cluster, thereby affirming their membership. Our spectroscopic observations also revealed the presence of two previously unknown blue straggler stars which will be further explored in future research.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called learning with initial knowledge. It has been observed that the transferability of pre-trained DNNs tends to decrease for downstream tasks that demand high levels of specificity and versatility. Consequently, there is a growing need to improve the transferability of pre-trained DNNs for all tasks. This two-part study focuses on the impact of data characteristics and initial model design on the transferability of Pre-LNs for down-stream tasks based on a MSE-based data characterization approach called Euclidean Distance. This technique analyzes feature extraction and classification as independent processes to determine whether back-propagation during refinement is beneficial based on certain criteria. It was observed that initial learning-based methods are inadequate due to certain flaws in common multi-layer model design. This led to the proposal of an innovative Gated MLP model to improve the initial generalization of Pre-LNs for down-stream tasks. Experiments were conducted using three Pre-LN-based methods, each with and without the proposed Gated model, to verify the efficacy of the new design. Results indicate that the proposed Gated model significantly improves the initial generalization of Pre-LNs, reducing their remaining shortcomings.

In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics in extensive networks, few studies have explored this phenomenon in networks comprised of multiple communities. This investigation delves into the fundamental principles of information diffusion in complex networks by incorporating basic assumptions into a model that enables simulation on modular networks. Through both theoretical analyses and computational simulations, we have derived insights into how network modularity affects diffuse information relevant to various applications. Furthermore, our results imply that the local structure of networks within individual communities, rather than global properties or random fluctuations, significantly influence information diffusion. Consequently, targeted information dissemination, such as through social mobilization programs or advertising campaigns, may be most effective when focused on community-level factors rather than global characteristics or minor individual network fluctuations.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and these measurements depend on how close those Lagrangian angles are to being perfectly aligned. Some outcomes resulting from these conditions are a definitive unique correspondence existing between one specified Lagrangian and its nearest neighbor under certain circumstances, and the total count of Lagrangian homotopy equivalences that can be constructed alongside their angular measurements.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, which involve modifying specific app fields such as package names, activity names, and intent filters to evade detection. Our research aims to explore effective methods to prevent problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices.

Service-oriented computing utilizes services to deliver business processes and systems with specific functionalities via standardized protocols. Traditionally, a cloud is perceived as an advanced service host offering on-demand computing resources, either as virtual machines or on a virtual network. The shift in perspective of services and clouds necessitates a fundamental change in how we refer to services, especially when used as building blocks for business processes and systems, to facilitate clear communication and understanding among technical, business, and executive stakeholders. This paper explores the definition, classification, examples, service discovery, and assessment methods for microservices, providing a comprehensive insight into this emerging topic.

Recent experimental observations supporting the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order are challenged by a reoccurring phase of unusual quantized nature, which is gapped in the thermodynamic limit.  Unlike other known phases such as Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, and PH-Pf phases, this new phase emerges at an intermediate mixing of Landau levels.  A proposed wave function accurately represents the unique topological properties of this phase by exhibiting distinct topological properties and agreeing with calculations under the thermal Hall effect, while also extending previous understanding of the Landau level degeneracy structure.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric are equivalent to those required for Kerr metric transformation, essentially reducing to the Kerr metric interpretation. Due to the Nature restrictions on exotic matter presence, the conditions necessary for Thakurta black hole formation are identical to those of the Kerr metric, indicating that Thakurta black holes are essentially a subset of the Kerr black holes and cannot form independently.

The complex disc structure and dynamics of protoplanetary discs enable the creation of pressure waves that play a significant role in planet formation. The stress caused by these pressure waves can extend deep into the disc, affecting areas with significant potential for planet development. The relationship between pressure bumps and planet formation is particularly noteworthy, and recent studies have explored how pressure waves influence the development of planet cores. The stress caused by a pressure wave can extend deep into the disc, significantly impacting areas where cores form. The development of planet cores relies on sufficient sedimentation and viscosity to reduce turbulence and enhance the core formation efficiency. The core formation efficiency also relies on the rate at which momentum is transferred from large to small scales. The momentum can be enhanced by increased viscosity, a process that relies on the disk's alpha parameter. The study found that core formation efficiency peaks at a specific alpha parameter value. The core formation efficiency also significantly increases when the radius of the core is large or has formed in areas with low momentum.

Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. Our investigation focuses on a well-known learning algorithm based on gradient descent and assesses its efficacy in a variety of learning problems under robust, computationally efficient conditions. Our analysis demonstrates that if the function being optimized is not well-behaved in terms of computational complexity, then a significant number of parameters is necessary for successful convergence, even when considering highly informative data. This highlights the potential for computational constraints to influence the necessity of massive models. Furthermore, our findings emphasize the significance of considering the algorithm in tandem with its environmental dependencies, as the same model can be effective or ineffective solely based on its choice of optimizer.

Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in threefold sumsets have been proven. More specifically, considering a countable discrete abelian group $G$ and commuting endomorphisms $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$ whose images have finite indices, we demonstrate that for any set $E \subset G$ with positive upper Banach density and satisfying the condition that the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms is zero, we find a set $F \subset E$ such that it has positive upper Banach density and the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms is a set containing a Bohr set. This generalizes the previous findings of Edmonds, Laakso and Voigt and Milovich. Furthermore, we provide analytical proofs for these results by adopting an almost periodicity approach rather than the initial nilpotent one.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We conducted an extensive computational analysis involving up to 120 customers and ten vehicles, revealing that our method consistently outperforms a traditional mixed-integer programming formulation by finding significantly more optimal solutions and tighter bounds.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with modality-noise and modality-missing. We introduce K3M, a novel method incorporating knowledge modality to mitigate noise and supplement missing modalities in image and text data. K3M incorporates a modal-encoding layer, a modal-interaction layer, and a modal-fusion layer, all guided by a knowledge-based objective in addition to a pretraining objective for cross-modal interaction, which combines image and text modality learning in a semi-synchronous manner. The proposed method outperforms existing techniques in dataset validation across sales, retrieval, and visual representation tasks.

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers promising possibilities for examining brain structure and function. Although still in its early stages, this method shows potential for visualizing unique patterns in brain data, making it attractive for supervised applications. A new formulation developed using the regularized kernel trick enables the creation of a closed-form solution for DIM and reveals its underlying similarities with other techniques, such as DeepSore, DeepCluster, and DeepEssence. By resolving DIM from a closed-form perspective, it becomes evident that it can be incorporated into supervised algorithms with only slight modifications, leading to significant improvements in performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches for supervised dimensionality reduction. The efficacy of this formulation is demonstrated by applying DIM to challenging tasks in supervised dimensionality reduction, where it achieves superior results compared to other techniques, such as DeepSore, DeepCluster, and DeepEssence.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents an innovative score called I-score, an efficient search algorithm termed Backward Dropping Algorithm, and an innovative feature engineering technique known as the "dagger technique." Firstly, the paper introduces I-score, an innovative score that identifies and assesses the influence of specific words within a text document on the classification outcome. This score enables researchers to understand word importance and develop novel feature engineering techniques. Secondly, the paper proposes an innovative search algorithm, Backward Dropping Algorithm, that simplifies I-score computation and improves efficiency. Lastly, the paper outlines an innovative "dagger" technique for feature engineering, which enhances the performance of text classification by improving the quality of the generated features. To validate performance, the proposed methods are applied to a range of text classification tasks, including 41 classification datasets from the UCI machine learning repository, and their effectiveness is demonstrated through comparison with standard feature engineering techniques. This work ultimately aims to improve four primary aspects of text classification: (a) understanding word importance, (b) improving I-score efficiency, (c) developing novel feature engineering techniques, and (d) enhancing overall text classification performance.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\lambda$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$, within a broad range in the paramagnetic phase, where $U'$ represents the inter-orbital interaction and $J'$ represents the pair hopping interaction. Increasing interactions within this phase causes a shift to a state characterized by orbital ordering. When the interactions exceed a certain threshold, symmetry is broken in the spin and orbital sectors, giving rise to a state characterized by ferromagnetic ordering. Under this condition, $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ becomes dependent on the interplay between the orbital's self-sir and spin-superposition conditions. Interestingly, $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ approaches 0 as interactions in the system increase. Furthermore, when compared to experimental observations, it has been found that orbital steering plays no significant role in explaining the experimentally-shown increase in the spin-polarized state's $\lambda$ constant.

A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
conformal transformation between the Einstein metric, where gravitons are normalised states,
and the Jordan metric governing the coupling between gravity and matter. This
secluded dark matter, isolated from the Standard Model by a large energy scale
$\Lambda$ above which the Jordan metric diverges from the Einstein metric, is
characterised by two key parameters: the mass $m_\chi$ and the decay width $\Gamma$
resulting from its rare couplings with Standard Model particles. With its lifetime
exceeding 70% of the age of the Universe at minimal coupling, this dark matter
candidate can be detected through its cosmic abundance and is suitable for the
study of dark matter with low mass and is anticipated in supergravity models at
low $\theta$ with the existence of a Higgsino with similar mass values.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments, accurately assessing their performance in the event of distribution shifts is crucial. Ways to measure the performance of these devices in shifted distributions exist; however, these methods lack theoretical connections, making it difficult to determine their reliability. This study establishes a limit on the performance of these evaluative methods when distribution changes occur, considering linear relationships between features and outcomes. Furthermore, it provides guidance on the creation of more reliable predictions in the event of distribution shifts, based on the study's findings.

High-fidelity simulations involving atomic-level detail are now widely available,
thanks to advancements in force fields that enable such simulations. Despite
these developments, there is still debate surrounding the issue of rotational
degrees of freedom in all-atom nucleic acid simulations. We have discovered that
it is feasible to implement six rotational parameters that can be employed
throughout a nucleic acid system consisting of multiple rings, thereby eliminating
the need for any constraints. This allows for realistic nucleotides with
freely rotating bases and phosphate links, as well as flexible sugar linkages and
a simulated bond representing the simulated bond between a nucleotide and
deoxyribose within a deoxyribonucleic acid base pair. Simulations utilizing
these settings have proven to minimize issues with nucleic acid topology in
recent simulations involving an 80-base piece of DNA and also successfully
replicated the structure of a nucleic acid (ATH) in an in vitro study, as well
