Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid employed simplified thermal conductivity and convective heat transfer assumptions, leading to inaccurate predictions. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis that accurately simulates the thermal behavior of the fluid and its impact on laser interactions. The study examines the diffracted beam in the far field produced by a laser entering the fluid, as well as the interferometric pattern formed perpendicular to the laser propagation axis. The results are validated against experimental findings, providing comprehensive insight into laser energy transfer and propagation through the fluid. The study also investigates the limit of laser energy transfer through the fluid and proposes a figure of merit to quantify this limit.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to specific design decisions for the extraction of valuable information. This is made possible by recognizing that discussing an issue serves the purpose of reaching a consensus on a course of action. This is akin to a English sentence that conveys a suggestion or direction, which can be mirrored in a dataset to facilitate the identification of design decisions and their underlying rationales. Comprehending these rationales can provide developers with a deeper understanding of design choices and motivate change. This study draws from a diverse collection of four discussion datasets, employing a machine learning model trained on annotated data to identify design decisions in unannotated discussions. This approach outperformed existing methods in three prediction metrics on four datasets and was applied in a study to examine how GitHub organizations make design decisions involving accessibility.

This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It integrates stream processing operators as cloud-based micro-services to facilitate the analysis and visualization of IoT-generated Big Data streams. H-STREAM's micro-services dynamically adjust their techniques according to the stream producers, data velocity, and available processing resources to ensure seamless processing and visualization of the streams. H-STREAM's effectiveness in tackling big stream and data processing challenges is demonstrated through its optimization of micro-service workflows, adaptive operator technologies, micro-service based stream scheduling, and stream visualization of high-speed IoT-generated data streams. Experimental findings demonstrate the benefits of H-STREAM in terms of execution time, processing efficiency, and overall performance.

The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers considerable detection possibilities. Though past research mainly focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings have uncovered a diverse and complex phenomenology associated with the non-resonant diagrams at narrow widths. In this study, we thoroughly examine the influence of the non-resonant diagrams on the single production topologies of Top and Bottom companions and their impact on estimating total production rates. Our findings indicate that the non-resonant diagrams can yield a considerable share of events, particularly for the Top companion at lower center-of-pilot energies and for both companions at the LHC. Notably, this phenomenon has significant implications for LHC searches for vector-like quark partners.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models has opened the door to automated query generation. Despite this significant advancement, SPARQL queries often feature variables that make completing the queries challenging for models trained on limited training data, necessitating sophisticated completion techniques. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a innovative approach called Top-K Resampling that capitalizes on the insights of expert human query generators by reordering the variables in a manner analogous to how humans order the variables, thereby enhancing the performance of both completion and generation tasks for NMT-based SPARQL generation.

This work introduces a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets in Computer Science. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and thousands of publishing venues based solely on available paper publication information. By treating authorship patterns at individual publishing venues as a predictive task and focusing on key performance metrics, our method generates high-accuracy quality scores for every recorded conference and journal. Furthermore, our scores can also be utilized to model and track shifts in field dynamics across different periods. In addition, our scores can serve as a basis for evaluating both individual researchers and academic institutions, demonstrating quantitative evaluations comparable to those derived from citation analysis or peer review processes. In contrast to many prevailing evaluation methods, our solution's reliance on extensive, publicly accessible data enables seamless replication and validation. In a collaborative spirit, our complete code and dataset have been shared publicly at https://github.com/leonidk/venue_scores for the purpose of facilitating further development upon this research.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated in related fields. These techniques are further applied to establish guarantees for systems that combine neural networks and control feedback loops. Ultimately, these tools facilitate the analysis of safe control systems and support deep reinforcement learning with robustness guarantees.

This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and addresses them within the context of a unified framework rooted in random process theory. Specifically, we draw from Jardine and Sibson's concept of an ideal partition, Topoleski's development of a clustering theory based on monotonically similar dissimilarities, and the sequential clustering paradigm established by Murdock. By interpreting these areas within a consistent framework, we highlight their interconnectedness, thereby providing a clearer understanding of their interrelations.

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. While existing methods successfully address certain structured tensor degeneracies, they fail to address others, leading to a need for novel approaches. Our new method, strucNet, addresses tensor completion degeneracies using a deep neural network that enhances low-rankness and identifies more complex pattern-based degeneracies within 4D tensors, specifically polarimetric hyperspectral images. This allows strucNet to handle a wide range of tensors, including those with synthetic aperture radar properties. By exploiting the tensor's intrinsic structure, strucNet completes and recovers degraded 4D data, demonstrating superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods through numerical evaluations.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type D. This finding has implications for the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_n$, revealing that these algebras have infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 3)$-dimensional Nichols algebra of type $(\mathfrak s \otimes \mathfrak s^*, \mathfrak m \otimes \mathfrak m^* )$; the $(4, 3)$-dimensional Nichols algebra of type $(\mathfrak s \otimes \mathfrak s^*, \mathfrak m \otimes \mathfrak \overline{m^* } )$; the $(5, 3)$-dimensional Nichols algebra of type $(\mathfrak s \otimes \mathfrak s^*, \mathfrak m \otimes \mathfrak m^* )$. This development answers an earlier question posed by Dolganova, Heinle, and Nicas.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic wave-like behavior. In a recent study, researchers used direct numerical simulations within a triaxial geometry to investigate the coexistence of these two contrasting forms of turbulence. Interestingly, it was found that one specific combination of angular momentum rates from the geostrophic and inertial regimes is capable of generating a unique bi-spectrum that lies at the interface of geostrophic and wave turbulence. This discovery implies that rotating turbulence is more complex than previously thought, with its characteristics depending heavily on the inertial rates and subject to change with varying scales of observation.

We propose a novel framework called Graph Normalization, aimed at mitigating the negative effects of large graph size on machine learning model performance when working with graph-based learning methods. Our framework utilizes a deep generative model to generate normalized graphs, where each node's degree is constrained, and we demonstrate that this problem can be viewed as sampling from a set of independent maximal subsets. Experiments conducted on a range of real-world datasets showcase the efficacy of our approach in enhancing the performance of advanced graph-based learning methods.

This research focuses on electrically modulated graphene in a parallel plate configuration under the assumption that a finite Rashba spin-orbit interaction is present. The study utilizes the Green's function method to derive magnetic and thermal properties for both graphene and a 2DEG in a square well potential. The intention is to assess how the presence of a spin-orbit interaction alters the thermal and magnetic properties previously established for 2DEG systems by Shevchik and Ziegler. Key differences between graphene and 2DEG are revealed through comparison of their properties, which includes the graphene's lack of linear Landau level behavior and the influence of the Dresselhaus term on graphene's thermal properties, particularly its spin and charge temperatures, as well as its Drude weight and longitudinal conductance.

Recent findings of low-frequency radio emissions from various nearby active star systems have sparked debate over their celestial origin. Experts are divided between attributing these emissions to magnetospheric phenomena similar to those observed in planets or friction between exoplanets and their host star's disk surface. To shed light on the source of these radio emissions, researchers analyzed data from the SETI Institute's Glueckman dataset and the Pulsar Search Collaboratory, covering 27 nearby active star systems, including several systems with detected radio emissions. To their surprise, researchers discovered narrow radio frequency signatures exceeding 3σ confidence that matched previously reported data for TRAPPIST-1e and TRAPPIST-1d. Additionally, researchers found multiple narrow frequency signatures exceeding 3σ confidence in systems K2-39b and L 98-59, with one of these signatures closely aligning with data released by the AAREX project; however, researchers couldn't confirm any matches with data released after 2021. Narrow radio frequency signatures, ranging from 0.1 to 40 kHz, were identified in active star systems with masses between 0.25 and 0.65 solar masses. Significantly, these frequencies were 1.5 to 13 times greater than planetary rotation rates, suggesting an atmospheric origin linked to exoplanets, while dispersions in frequency also increased with system distance, suggesting interference based on line-of-sight measurements, not planetary size. By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational resources and visual quality. The
approach relies on pre-computed neural networks for geometric and appearance properties
of 3D models, augmenting rendered images with a high-level of detail. For complex
models such as virtual human avatars, additional precision is needed for articulation
and expression data, necessitating a more sophisticated rendering method. To address
this, we have developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new pipeline that integrates
neural networks for virtual human avatars in a timely and efficient manner. Our
technique enhances visual quality, improves rendering speed and provides high-fidelity
articulation information, making it a superior alternative to alternative methods. We
demonstrate the capabilities of our approach in a range of applications, including
real-time streaming at high bitrates, telepresence, and movie production. Our work
demonstrates a significant improvement in rendering time and visual quality when compared
to existing solutions. Additionally, our technique allows for the creation of high-quality
virtual humans that meet the standards of the entertainment industry. Our code has been
made publicly available to provide a foundation for the development of new research
projects.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily offer a superficial similarity to the primate visual system. They do not address the fundamental question of how these two systems compare in terms of visual information processing. We developed a new method to analyze the distortions introduced by ANNs at an underlying neural level, mimicking the way neurons interact in animal visual systems. This method examines the generalization capabilities of both human and ANN systems within a specific task - object recognition. We applied this approach to a database containing natural images with varying levels of difficulty and identified key aspects of classification uncertainty in humans and ANNs. Interestingly, despite outperforming both systems in terms of generalization performance, ANNs fall short when tested under more complex image conditions, similar to suboptimal performance observed in humans. Additionally, our analysis revealed that both human and ANN uncertainty signals share similarities with those found in primate early visual system responses. These findings suggest that future advancements in machine learning should strive to mimic the interconnectivity between primate visual areas as well as the flexible information processing observed in humans.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the quantized Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses the $SU(2)$ quantum group, is a key concept in this field. The algebra's generators are linked to the Chern-Simons Lagrangian's combined cyclic variables and quantum factors through this connection. The Chern-Simons theory's Wilson line and its holomorphic counterpart generate the algebra, with the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant showing a holomorphic determinant weighting effect. This linking concept offers opportunities for further study in relation to the algebra's parameters, thereby extending previously established results for points arranged in a tetrahedral pattern, with analogous findings evident for the p-adic versions.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. Specifically, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of a strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the previously proposed triangle-square lattice model relevant to La4Cu3MoO12, leveraging a trimer-cluster based computational basis to avoid the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem at any finite temperature. Our analysis extends beyond the thermodynamic properties to examine the mean field theory prediction of a phase transition associated with chiral order. We observed the distinct formation of two peaks in the specific heat as well as the occurrence of degasculation and the mercedes sign patterns at low temperatures.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. For instance, to determine the sentiment of a given text simply provides it to GPT-3 without explicitly mentioning the task. This phenomenon prompts the question of why it occurs and whether it will persist. Research suggests that the internal representation of words in language models reflects their probable meanings, likely resulting in coherent generalizations. Additionally, fine-tuning these models on labeled data enhances zero-shot performance. We refer to the process of adjusting the word representations as "meta-tuning." To examine the link between meta-tuning and zero-shot performance, we designed a basic task that requires models to identify words with multiple meanings (e.g., "bank" referring to either "financial institution" or "riverbank"). We studied how modifying the word representations impacts zero-shot performance on more intricate tasks like recognizing financial institutions and understanding phrases with multiple meanings. Our results demonstrate that meta-tuning not only improves zero-shot performance but also makes it more stable to various changes in the model's word representations. Furthermore, we identified a connection between meta-tuning and the phenomenon of concept drift in existing research on explaining language models.

In depth research into the link between the first-order electroweak phase transition and electroweak baryogenesis has been examined through a theoretical framework that accounts for strong first-order transitions and realistic lattice Higgs models, which often feature moderate first-order transitions. This investigation found that such transitions can enable sufficient gravitational waves production that may be detectable by future cosmological probes, specifically by PING and CosmoZA, two gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, Higgs interactions during the phase transition can be enhanced to a level that may be within the scope of detection by future 100 TeV particle accelerators, such as the proposed FCC-hh, through observation of associated gamma-z boson pairs.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring spectroscopic redshifts and optimizes future observations to maximize the proportion of robust redshifts. To facilitate this process, a publicly accessible code is shared at (https://github.com/tjlcbakx/redshift-search-graphs). We discuss scenarios in which robust redshifts can be confidently identified through single-line or multiple-line measurements, as well as instances where redshift ambiguity persists despite multiple line detections. Our analysis leverages the redshift distribution of millimeter and submillimeter samples to assess the efficiency of various observational practices, including those utilizing interferometers and dedicated redshift machines. Finally, we outline the requirements for achieving robust redshifts (> 80%) in the submillimeter spectrum, including the need for high-resolution measurements of the 12.7 um fine-structure line or the 3 beta-emission lines in certain objects.

This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice with antiferromagnetic properties. A highly complex phase diagram arises from the lattice due to the conflicting interactions between adjacent spins and their neighbors. By simulating both the ordered 120-degree phase and a potential spin liquid phase at a specific ratio of $J_2/J_1$, we are able to identify the nature of the low-energy excitations in each. It was found that the 120-degree phase exhibits a unique spin liquid characteristic with a spin-1 excitation, separate from the spin-1/2 degeneracy characteristic of the spin liquid phase at the specified $J_2/J_1$ ratio. Two distinct low-energy excitations were also identified in the spin liquid phase, featuring a relationship with a low-energy continuous spin-1/2 excitation and a much more energetic spin-1 excitation. A substantial amount of energy is required to transform the former into the latter. Near the critical point separating the two phases, a unique spin liquid phase emerges with three low-energy degenerate modes, corresponding to a much lighter low-energy excitation. A much heavier low-energy excitation was found to have no influence on the ground state in the spin liquid phase under certain conditions. The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on $Z_3$ symmetry, where a complex triplet Higgs boson has no initial mass and interaction. By regulating lattice size through variations in $N_\tau$, the investigation reveals that the phase transition depends on this regulation: crossover transitions occur when there are 2 sites and the phase transitions turn first-order for 3 sites and more. Moreover, thermal properties of the Higgs field exhibit contrasting behaviors based on its initial mass: when massive, the phase transition changes based on the lattice regulation while having no mass results in a fixed phase transition picture regardless.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in the study of antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its in-plane N\'{e}el vector degeneracy. This study focuses on growing Cr$_2$Al crystals and examining its magnetic properties as a function of orientation. Using neutron diffraction and simulations, the research finds that Cr$_2$Al has a magnetic ordering identical to Mn$_2$Au and is likely to provide new insights into spintronics through comparison with MoSi$_2$-type structure materials. The results from various measurements and simulations confirm that the system exhibits a single ordering phase transition, no spin canting, and an in-plane N\'{e}el vector temperature of $634 \pm 2$ K. The findings of this research match well with predictions made using simulations and further support the system's unique characteristics when studied as a function of orientation.

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating essential collision characteristics, while also ensuring the conservation of momentum and energy. Based on this $
u$-model, a first-order numerical framework is developed and tested against various benchmark tests to assess its accuracy, particularly in comparing its results with Boltzmann's solution and existing kinetic models under different rarefied flow conditions.

Voice assistant applications like Alexa and Google Assistant significantly benefit from advancements in data-driven semantic parsing, a foundational step that translates spoken language into meaningful instructions into the appropriate programming language. To bridge the gap between spoken and written languages, precise knowledge representation is crucial. This study introduces an innovative approach to semi-supervised refinement of low-quality knowledge-based data by leveraging conditional models that generate knowledge-based data. The proposed method specifically identifies and rectifies incorrect knowledge-based sentences tied to particular entities. Building upon this idea, a new model called KRS (Knowledge-Related Sentence) is presented, aiming to generate corrected knowledge-based sentences as alternatives. The model incorporates the concept of mutual reinforcement, where the annotation of a sentence influences and improves its related neighbors, fostering a back-and-forth exchange of knowledge between annotated and unannotated pairs. Evaluations conducted on the popular MenuPAI dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing non-semi-supervised techniques and approaches that rely solely on pre-trained language models.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine crucial information, precise measurements of heavy quark particles and jets are vital to understand how energy distribution works at high-energy collisions and to learn about the strengths of quarks within protons and nuclei. To achieve this goal, researchers will conduct an in-depth study of open and hidden charm hadrons, as well as their relationships with the underlying parton distribution functions, utilizing cutting-edge detector technology and breakthroughs in data collection techniques.

A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four galaxies - 4U1846-365, MAXI J0637-472, MAXI J2123+504, and GX 401k- Is discussed. These patterns, identified through BHSRC analysis, were found on frequencies of 0.1 - 12 Hz and lasted from 5 - 155 days. This discovery confirms that each galaxy displays similar patterns, known as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs). Unlike Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs), which have stronger correlations with black hole mass and which states they occur in, the characteristics of QPEs vary greatly. In some cases, they display steady-state variability, while in others, they are associated with changes in other patterns. This suggests that QPEs may be influenced by different mechanisms, such as the migration of accretion hot spots, in relation to black hole mass and which state they are in.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research provides new evidence from spectropolarimetric analysis on how the strength of a magnetic field in HD58260, a magnetic star, varies with altitude in its atmosphere. The results suggest that the magnetic field in HD58260 is approximately 0.9 kilotesla in the lower atmosphere but significantly weaker, at less than 0.1 its surface value, in the upper layers. A model based on the model atmosphere for normal stars reveals that the variation in the field's strength is likely due to the mixing of magnetic and non-magnetic gas over time. Notably, the findings present a challenge to hydrodynamic models of the atmosphere, which previously predicted that the magnetic field in HD58260 would be zero at the upper layer due to a different gradient. A second model using the ATLAS9 program also showed that the variation in the field's strength could be explained if the gas in the upper atmosphere was cooler than expected.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques. Based on these findings, we suggest that H30α is a reliable proxy for the SFR of low-mass, metal-poor, and star-forming galaxies. In the case of NGC 5253, the SFR derived from ALMA's data is consistent with that based on photometry and far-infrared (FIR) emission, but significantly lower than that estimated from radio continuum and Hα emission. The SFR discrepancy in NGC 5253 is similar to that observed in the metal-poor galaxy IC 10 and can be attributed to the lower oxygen abundance in H30α-emitting regions, which results in lower dust abundance and a reduced radio-to-IRX ratio. This indicates that the SFR measured using H30α, radio continuum, and Hα emissions is significantly lower than that derived from FIR and dust-based SFR indicators. This discrepancy also leads to an underestimation of SFR derived from prolonged ALMA observing time, as more intense regions contribute more to the SFR but have lower gas fractions. Therefore, SFR indicators based on gas-to-dust ratios may produce biased estimates. In the case of galaxies like NGC 5253 with low metallicities, their SFRs are likely underestimated, which

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite group, or the direct product of two integer groups, especially when these are embedded in a given space as discrete.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under a prior distribution, which it isn't absolutely continuous with respect to. Utilizing the use of Hilbert--Schmidt operators allows us to establish a direct relationship between the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator, which describes the time-evolution of a quantum system, and the rates at which $P$ approximates $\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]$ for certain functions $f$. This connection is rooted in the fact that $P$ corresponds to the superoperator that describes the evolution of the quantum state $\rho(X,y)$ over time. Our findings are further supported by numerical estimates for specific systems. These results have significant implications in quantum-quantum correspondence theory. The utility of these results is further demonstrated in two specific applications where they are shown to be effective in reducing the computational complexity of certain problems.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, it demonstrates and illustrates the necessary and sufficient conditions for the associated error equations using a recently proposed method.

Recent studies have shown that incorporating the temporal context of facts in KGE can lead to better results in subsequent applications. However, existing methods achieve this by using the temporal scope across the entire knowledge graph, which can be computationally expensive and inefficient for large graphs. Our solution enables selection of relevant temporal context facts on a per-entity basis using a distance-based approach. In our framework, each entity maintains a temporal scope of facts and can be adapted to include or exclude facts from the temporal context. Our method enhances the expressive power of the framework by using the same terms to describe both entity characteristics and temporal scope associations. Our experiments using the Wikidata dataset demonstrate that this framework significantly outperforms existing temporal KGE methods in link prediction tasks and shows that our method can be applied to various knowledge graphs with impressive results, even when scaled up to larger graphs like Wikipedia.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned diverse applications, with theoretical understanding rooted in conventional beam propagation analysis. However, established frameworks are often insufficient for handling the extreme demands of high-power oscillators. This study expands upon the ABCD-matrix method to investigate ring resonators in high-power settings, also offering critical guidance for maintaining stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-power pulse applications.

Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (ASO-Fed), we employed an online paradigm that sends participants' gradients instead of the complete updated model. Despite this, participant heterogeneity and asynchronous data transmission introduce bias within participants' model updates, referred to as asynchronous bias, thus requiring mitigation. To address this bias, we developed an asynchronous bias correction (ABC) method that combines two approaches: correcting the bias at the participant level and combining participants' updates at the server level. Experimental results show that while ASO-Fed reduces communication overhead, it is more susceptible to asynchronous bias. The proposed ABC method effectively eliminates the asynchronous bias, providing insights into the impact of communication delay on federated learning and how to rectify issues arising from communication shortcomings.

To optimize thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption through their back side, researchers investigated metal, semitransparent and dielectric thin films with numerical methods. The study on metal films was followed by an investigation of photonic band gap crystal pseudo-perfect mirrors, revealing a 0.4% higher maximum absorption within the 600-900nm wavelength range in comparison to metal films. Thin and bremsstrüller dielectric films with high absorption were found to decrease this advantage to 0.2% in presence of these photonic crystals. Although very thin bremsstrüller dielectric films show improved absorption properties at certain optimized thicknesses of less than 1nm, the improved absorption in bremsstrüller dieuchs is not recommended for practical solar cell designs, given its excessive absorption of charge carriers to reach such thinness. The charge carrier absorption in bremsstrüller dieuchs is found to be as high as 30% at 1nm and increases exponentially with thinner pseudo-perfect dieuchs, in contrast to a much slower decrease in absorption of photons, or pabs, within 100-900nm wavelength range. The experimental realization of these extremely thin pseudo-perfect dieuchs is discussed as well as the proposed alternative methods to achieve improved absorption in thin-film silicon solar cells.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, approach certain iterated exponential functions. This development complements recent findings of K. Matvievskaya and M. Nakano. In this context, our goal is to establish a link between the properties of these holomorphic functions in the upper half-plane and the behavior of certain entire functions, specifically Siegel-Gel'fand-Malgrange filters. This in turn enables us to derive information about holomorphic extensions of iterated exponentials, which in turn allows us to discuss certain holomorphic dynamical systems.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science, yet current construction methods are somewhat limited. Our technique enables the creation of high dimensional expanders with a minimal number of vertices, based on a given graph's properties. Moreover, we can generate random objects, such as Ramanujan graphs, in the form of high dimensional expanders.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an "up-up-down" arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in the magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the presence of inevitable defects and resulting in a significant residual term in the Curie-Weiss temperature. A theoretical model incorporating the effects of these defects was employed to maximize the underlying frustration within the system, consistent with the experimental results for the crystalline properties and magnetic arrangements in GdInO3.

The application of graph embedding for predicting links in sparse networks has been relatively limited, primarily due to the scarcity of nodes and connections within these networks. We've introduced Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel scheme that creates an embedding suitable for large sparse networks. SSNE starts by converting a sparse graph into a series of triangles, then employs a low-dimensional representation of these triangles as the final embedding. Unlike existing methods, SSNE encodes not only the geometric structure but also the structural properties of these triangles in the embedding matrix. Through theoretical analysis, we've found that this embedding preserves the intrinsic structural characteristics of the input graph. Furthermore, we've discovered that triangle-based embedding possesses better generalization performance on label prediction compared to node representation. Experimental results on four sparse networks have demonstrated the efficacy of SSNE in predicting labels compared to other leading node embedding algorithms.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 6mm deep silicon etch, overcoming depth limitations and enabling the creation of a deep atomic vapor cell. Although initial vapor cell designs had minimum feature sizes limited to 1.5mm, a novel two-cell configuration was developed with a 25mm separation between the cells, utilizing silicon waflets with 6mm thickness and wafer diameters of 76mm. This enabled the manufacturing of multiple vapor cells with each wafer, reducing the reliance on costly microfluidic devices and flexible substrates with questionable performance. By implementing a selective alignment process, the growth direction of the crystals is optimized, resulting in 98% crystals growing perpendicular to the substrate. By analyzing the frequency shift, a high Q value of around 38000 was found for the 132Xe island of interest. By comparing the measured linear isotopic shift with predicted values, the starting isotopic composition of the 132Xe island was estimated, showing a rich isospin space with possible natural compositions. This serves as a starting point for future natural Xe island research focused on quantum logic applications.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property loss, and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thereby offering superior performance and reduced error rates compared to current methods. Although DL-based image fusion methods have been well-documented, they have yet to be applied in the fire detection context, and the sector still grapples with fundamental questions regarding data quality, the efficacy of traditional evaluation metrics, and the need for human oversight in DL-based systems. This study addresses these concerns by proposing a novel framework for wildfire detection utilizing a deep learning-based image fusion approach. To establish a benchmark, we evaluate three prominent fire detection models alongside six image fusion techniques with various wildfire-related datasets. Our study reveals that a DL-based fusion approach outperforms traditional methods and significantly reduces errors, albeit with increased computational demands. Nevertheless, when combining detection and fusion algorithms, the speed disparity becomes less pronounced, underscoring the importance of each component in the overall system.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe repercussions, making the utilization of social media a great approach to identify individuals experiencing depression and connect them with a specialist depression counselor. Although traditional methods rely on comprehensive diagnostic manuals, the task becomes complicated due to the difficulty in collecting social media data from depression patients. Moreover, such datasets are challenging to annotate due to the absence of depression symptoms in data and the need to correctly represent depression levels. This study aims to address these challenges by introducing a multi-class dataset for depression levels derived from social media data. Furthermore, the study proposes a novel depression identification method that employs a dual encoder approach, with one encoder trained to capture general depression features and the other trained to find unique depression features within each level. This method allows the model to determine depression levels on social media posts, and it outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches while providing insights into depression counseling.

We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, including correlation functions and probability distributions. These models, which build on existing work and incorporate lockdown measures and the critical role of hospitals and health care facilities, enable us to simulate two scenarios. One scenario considers the SIS model, which reveals that the coronavirus spread can be halted by removing lockdown measures but necessitates an infinite number of lockouts if no measures are taken. A more comprehensive model, which includes hospitals and health care facilities and is based on the SIS triad, enables us to investigate the impact of these services on the pandemic. This model, which handles limited hospital capacity and intra-rational behavior, indicates that the virus can't be eradicated through lockups and that an optimal level of hospital capacity exists that minimizes outbreak severity. We've verified these findings by validating the model's correlation functions and probability distributions against real-world data.

The ISGMR and a $K = 0$ component of the prolate giant dipole resonance in well-deformed $^{184,186,192}$W nuclei were investigated through (alpha, alpha') reactions at beam energies corresponding to the quasielastic region. An ISGMR peak was detected at 1099, 1101, and 1121 MeV, along with a distinct low-lying isoscalar monopole peak at 783 MeV, strongly indicating that this phenomenon is closely linked to the incompressibility modulus and energy cutoff parameter. Additionally, the broadness of the ISGMR resonances in these nuclei appears to be influenced largely by high density and non-linear density terms.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an asymptote, for a broad class of position-dependent friction models, is established. Additionally, it is found that any system path will converge asymptotically towards the optimal solution path, which is the path that reaches the attractable region in the shortest time. Brief explanations of the practical implications of these findings are also provided.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, options, and taking into account factors such as trading costs, liquidity constraints and other frictions. This algorithm can effectively handle portfolios of any nature and features the ability to adapt to time-dependent volatility conditions. Most notably, our approach allows for optimal hedging strategies to be learned without prior knowledge of the underlying price dynamics, thereby overcoming the limitations associated with parameter estimation errors in traditional mathematical finance models. By testing our approach on various market environments characterized by different levels of volatility and financial instability, we evaluate its performance and examine how factors such as the type of trading costs, availability of borrowing and short selling opportunities influence the resulting outcomes.

The ever-expanding options available to users has created insatiable demand for personalized recommendations across an ever-growing array of choices. As a result, a recent area of focus within the research community has been on the development of recommender systems that leverage emerging technologies such as graph neural networks, meta-learning, and natural language processing. These systems utilize explicit user characteristics such as age, gender, and interests, as well as implicit activities such as item ratings and click history. To build upon existing expertise, a comprehensive examination of the underlying technologies and explicit/implicit data in the context of recommender systems has been undertaken. This survey aims to explore how data-driven approaches can inform recommendation, with a particular emphasis on the synergies between explicit and implicit signals. To set the stage for these discussions, a thorough review of existing recommenders and related data collection methods will be presented, accompanied by a detailed analysis of global implicit data and recommendation patterns.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. The Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of this particular DCHE has five distinct singular points: three located near a vanishing parameter value, one corresponding to infinity, and another positioned at its reciprocal, as well as a fifth point at infinity. The monodromy matrix of the equation near a specific regular resonant singularity can be observed to consist of a particular matrix combination involving matrices associated with other singularities, based on a recently established theorem. The applicability of this theorem has been extended to incorporate previously excluded cases, enabling the identification of all resonances present in the equation for each specific singularity. The parabolic case possesses a single resonance at 1/2, a case often represented by the Meromorphic equation. The equation's unfolding along two distinct trajectories, in conjunction with its uniformization, has been successfully applied to determine the list of all resonances in the equation for each specific singularity. The obtained results have been further generalized for the class of reducible double confluent Heun equations having $k \geq 2$ and $\kappa \geq 2$.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the case of a non-smooth observation model, where data blocks are observed at different noise levels for a non-Gaussian distribution under minimal assumptions. We derive exact formulas for the minimum number of data samples required for perfect recovery, based on the matrix's intrinsic properties. These results have far-reaching implications for several applications, including analysis of multi-task learning, polynomial regression, and computation of the total correlation for non-Gaussian random variables.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its behavior at critical points where rotations become restricted. These rotational limitations give rise to distinct critical energies related to an isolated rotational mode. To describe the vibrational behavior, we extend the Stokes theorem to a two-dimensional phase space defined by angular momentum and a pseudangle, and, for the first time, calculate the complete spectrum, revealing a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with unique characteristics in the complex plane. This yields a distinct exceptional point at a particular complex phase, and a symmetry-broken symmetry point with far-reaching implications for determining the system's charges in relation to an exceptional point. Moreover, we develop a strategy for identifying an exceptional point based on a single experimentally measurable frequency.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value, $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$, is observed.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding for each voxel. A fully connected layer dynamically selects and combines these embeddings, and a classifier determines the final diagnosis. By integrating this scheme with double feature extraction, we've enhanced the diagnosis accuracy to 0.8519 AUC, outperforming current top methods.

Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing chemical reactions, biological pathways, social connections, and other intricate relationships. Mastering network science necessitates the mastery of a comprehensive toolkit spanning numerous fields of study, including graph and probability theory, linear algebra, machine learning, combinatorics, and statistical physics.

This comprehensive resource is designed to provide foundational knowledge of this toolkit, serving as an introductory guide for students and a reference for practitioners across diverse fields including computer science, data science, social network analysis, network biology, civil engineering, and other related disciplines. Covering a broad range of topics, these chapters are written by prominent experts in network science, who offer unique perspectives stemming from their individual areas of study. Despite its broad scope, this book aims to offer a systematic approach to understanding network science, beginning with the basic principles and gradually exploring more advanced concepts and current research areas.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is incomplete and that there are three key areas to consider: 1) global changes happening over longer periods; 2) slow-changing processes influencing ecological and evolutionary changes; and 3) feedbacks between these different timescales of change. By broadening our view of time scales, we gain a more comprehensive understanding of how changes occur and can predict a wider range of outcomes. This expanded perspective also enables a deeper exploration of the role of stability in systems undergoing evolution, including the potential for complex dynamics to emerge.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can excel in multiple downstream tasks with little adaptation, SUPERB highlights a significant paradigm in the speech field that needs to be studied more. Specifically, assessing the ability of speech models to resist malicious attacks under the control of knowledgeable and inexperienced adversaries has become a high priority in the speech community. In this research, we make a first effort to test the potential vulnerability of speech models to adversarial attacks. We first develop advanced attacks tailored to two types of adversaries. We then assess the effect of these attacks on the speech models in the SUPERB benchmark. Our research finds that even slight alterations introduced by these attacks can greatly decrease speech classification accuracy. Furthermore, we discover that advanced attacks from less knowledgeable adversaries have a greater impact than those from knowledgeable adversaries. We also find that including untargeted attacks in speech models results in less robust performance compared to including targeted attacks. Interestingly, we find that randomly altering speech a limited number of times can be as destructive as carefully altering speech as targeted attacks, suggesting that speech models can easily be manipulated by unauthorised parties.

Our research focuses on the theoretical underpinnings of Automated Market Makers, a core aspect of Decentralized Finance. We establish a mathematical framework and statistical tools to analyze the behavior of token price correlations within these systems. Our data-driven analysis reveals that token exchange rate volatility is the primary factor contributing to liquidity risk and arbitrage opportunities in certain corridors. Moreover, tokens with higher volatility are more likely to experience prolonged volatility periods, which we predict will lead to increased arbitrage risks within the AMM system.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. In this research, we develop a practical methodology for performing Sensitivity Analysis in the context of incomplete data and focus on the linear regression setting. Our methodology begins by identifying a set of plausible values for key parameters based on expert opinions, followed by a quantitative analysis of the impact of varying these parameters on the primary research findings. The results of our approach are demonstrated using real-world data from a study examining the efficacy of exercise in preventing or delaying the onset of dementia. Our methodology allows for the creation of a report highlighting potential weaknesses in the conclusions drawn from the data, as well as recommendations for improving the accuracy of future meta-analyses through enhancements to study reporting standards.

This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}\big]$. Firstly, prior research by the author concerning symmetries involving the Cartan generator(s) with non-trivial action, and those exhibiting generic behavior, are revisited and verified. A thorough enumeration is presented for non-generic symmetries, specifically those with purely diagonal actions. It is demonstrated that non-generic symmetries can be equivalent to ones involving the non-trivial Cartan generator(s) when certain transformations are applied within the quantum plane. These transformations include reflections, mirroring the concept of the involution seen in the classical case, and the normalized change of basis for the generator(s) exhibiting non-trivial action. Building on this, general formulas are established for expressing quantum determinants in terms of monocalistic operators, thereby achieving an exhaustive classification of non-generic $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs challenges.

The ALICE experiment has recorded the $p_\mathrm{T}$ distribution of D meson production, including both prompt and non-prompt (formed in beauty-hadron decays), in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, and focused on data with an integrated luminosity of approximately 19.3 nb^-1. D mesons were identified through their decays into different hadronic combinations, such as $\mathrm{D^0 \to K^-\pi^+}$ and $\mathrm{D_s^+\to \phi\pi^+\to K^-K^+\pi^+}$ and their conjugates. The cross section results of this analysis have better coverage and lower uncertainty than previous studies at the same rapidity range, enabling a more precise estimation of D meson integrated cross sections. The data also indicates that strange and non-strange fragmentation of charm and beauty quarks are similar and comparable to previous studies at other energies. The production rate of beauty-quark pairs at midrapidity is determined from non-prompt D meson measurements to be about 34.5 ± 2.4 (statistical) ± 4.7 (total systematic) microbarn.

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a study conducted on professional developers in Python revealed a lower incidence of insecure code for crypto-related tasks. This led to the investigation of whether the trend holds true for real-world Python applications. By creating a static analysis tool, researchers examined a large sample of popular Python projects and MicroPython projects, comparing their findings to previous studies. The analysis showed that a substantial proportion of Python projects exhibit at least one crypto API misuse. Similarities exist between the misuses encountered in Python and those found in other languages, including the excessive use of fixed diffusion values and inadequate salt usage. The study's data suggests that a major part of the crypto API misuse issue is attributable to Diffie-Hellman key exchange, rather than random diffused values, and that both non-technical and technical factors contribute to this phenomenon. The study implies that more targeted educational efforts may be necessary to effectively combat crypto API misuse.

This paper introduces an innovative technique for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan settings using machine learning techniques. Our approach builds upon a basic computer vision method known as End-to-End MEst, incorporating enhancements to deal with the distortions that occur when geolocation data is sent over long distances using GPS. Our research demonstrates that MEst can effectively pinpoint landmarks to within a meter, even in environments where the method's underlying assumptions are not met. By combining MEst with a simple neural network, we achieve an unprecedented level of precision, reaching an accuracy of just 0.65 and 1.20 meters in experiments conducted on public datasets for GPS-imperfect settings. Furthermore, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, delivering a more reliable result with significantly fewer necessary data points.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm utilizing proximal averaging that can be reformatted as a trainable neural network, optimizing through data-driven training. Our effectiveness is proven through numerical tests in various settings.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded, singular, or invertible within the context of BMOA_p.

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT content. This approach allows for numerical computation of all conformal data solely based on low-energy eigenstates, a method that was verified in the Ising and XXZ models. Additionally, we used this method to study the Haagerup model and determined the central charge and lowest scaling dimension of a specific spin-1 operator.

Creating accurate part-of-speech tags for texts written in historical languages is a difficult task due to limited dictionaries from that time period. Unlike current tagging systems, a new tagging system, developed in a data-driven manner, can identify the correct tags for ancient and medieval texts, but its application to Renaissance and Baroque texts is still a challenge. This study takes advantage of available tagging systems from languages that influenced the language of texts written during those times to improve the accuracy of such models. The project focuses on texts written in German, English, Italian, and other languages between the 8th and 20th centuries. The research team used a data-driven approach to improve the accuracy of models based on neural networks by fine-tuning them using training data with corrected tags, then comparing the performance of models trained with and without tagging system dictionaries from languages that influenced the language of texts written during those times. The results show that using training data with corrected tags provides more value than using training data with large language models and that the application of a model trained for one language to describe another from a similar time period is more accurate than trying to tag texts written in languages that influenced the language of texts written in different time periods.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a demand function candidate must meet. First, it must be symmetrical and have a negatively semi-definite Slutsky matrix, and second, it must be a unique concave solution to a specific partial differential equation globally. Additionally, under certain assumptions, the resulting utility function corresponds to a unique upper semi-continuous weak order, which we also show to be the only weak order under these assumptions. Our results are applied to econometric theory in several ways. First, we demonstrate that a converging sequence of demand functions converges to a valid demand function under specified conditions. Second, the space of uniformly Lipschitz demand functions on compact sets is complete. Finally, our utility function mapping becomes continuous when a specific additional condition is met, allowing a demand function's consistent estimation to lead to a utility function's consistent estimation.

As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from written English text. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for formalizing smart city needs, which effectively bridges language gaps and resolves common data inconsistencies. The purpose of this research is to explain CitySpec's functionality by showcasing three practical applications on diverse and relatively small datasets containing demands related to parking, building management, and emergency response.

Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variance reduction that leverages hidden inverse matrices, particularly suited for use with quantum computers. This method is compatible with a broad range of algorithms based on the Ruminant Riemannian Conjugate Gradient, including those used for log-determinant estimation and Gibbs' sampling in complex statistical models. Byinducing controlled errors in these algorithms, we successfully mitigate the negative effects of phase errors and inaccuracies in the Hessian tensor, as well as improve the distribution sampling process. Utilizing the RCG algorithm, we estimate the $n$-th root of a complex matrix with higher precision in a fixed number of iterations. This method involves incorporating hidden inverse matrices, which proves particularly efficient for determinantal processes. We showcase the potential of this technique in various practical applications, such as determining the spectral norms of matrices, estimating the statistical influence matrices of random walks on graphs, and sampling from complex multivariate statistical distributions by combining multiple determinantal processes. This last application is particularly noteworthy, as it offers a quantum speedup over the best known classical algorithms based on the Harer polynomial.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order results in a category with copowers, which are the pushed-forward category. We have a finding that in a regular category, the direct image of a partial order's greatest element corresponds to the greatest direct image of partial orders. For regular categories with infinitary lawfully ordered categories, the direct image of a partial order's greatest element is the greatest direct image of partial orders. We have a significant result that in the case of regular categories, the direct image of a partial order's greatest element is the greatest direct image of partial orders.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data. Analysis involves standardizing wind speeds from CERRA-2 and wave heights from ERS-2, then using an extreme value model combined with a non-stationary dependence measure to identify links between wind and wave patterns. The results from this analysis indicate a weakening relationship between wind and wave extremes in the North East Atlantic, which may have implications for weather forecasting and coastal engineering projects.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual-textual alignment for CLIP models on various tasks, we introduce a technique that refines image-text cross-modality learning via VT-CLIP. This process involves utilizing attention-driven mechanisms to direct text features toward informative visual regions, effectively enhancing visual-textual correlation for improved category-based matching. Subsequently, we demonstrate VT-CLIP's efficacy in few-shot classification scenarios on 11 prominent datasets.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study addresses the issue of reducing error in a linear system affected by uncertainty. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 elliptic operator shifting framework, we extend this concept to nonsymmetric matrices. Our innovation lies in the development of an operator shifting technique for matrix inverses, which is akin to the James-Stein estimator. This approach entails shifting the estimated inverse matrix in a particular direction to minimize average error. Our research explores the applicability of this technique in the nonsymmetric case, particularly in situations where shifting towards the origin does not always reduce error, unlike in the elliptic case. However, under specific conditions, similar to the elliptic case, the optimal shift is parallel to the noise vector and is proportional to the noise level. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by computational results that indicate that this technique may yield inverse matrices with reduced error at minimal computational cost.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered, and the equivariance group in question is the quaternionic group $Q_8$. In the process, we compute the Mackey functors for $\underline{\pi}_{k\rho} H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$.

Consider a Noetherian local ring R of characteristic p. For a division ring F of characteristic p, we establish the conditions under which the ring R will be F-rational, based on the properties of its extended fraction field. These conditions are similar to those that define the notion of weakly F-pure rings, potentially extending a prior result for rational extensions. Additionally, we find that certain ideal properties, such as weakly F-pure or subextension properties, are preserved under certain operations like polarization and dilution in characteristic p, yet this trait does not translate to the concept of quaternionic rationality in ring theory.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based ML projects frequently being open-source and widely shared, integrating ML models into clinical environments is typically restricted due to the vast amount of data and the associated security requirements.  The standardization of medical imaging and data exchange, achieved through DICOM, poses additional obstacles in terms of data analysis.  This study investigates ML applications within the context of diagnostic radiology and presents open-source solutions for data analysis, taking into account the specific constraints of this domain.  The goal of this work is to provide an overview of the current state of ML projects in diagnostic radiology, to highlight the importance of data normalization, and to suggest potential applications of ML in this field, while also addressing related challenges and future research opportunities.

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action when expressed in terms of a metric tensor, demonstrating that the surface charge resulting from its evaluation on the horizon is equivalent to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. This outcome is independent of the expression used for the Einstein action. Similar analysis for the Klein-Gordon and Rarita-Schwinger fields shows that their surface charges, when applied to a Killing horizon, mirror the corresponding bulk entropies in their respective theories.

In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model is applied in an unsupervised manner to derive a standardized, fixed-dimensional latent representation for long and variable DNA sequences. The resulting latent representation is then evaluated for a supervised task - splice site classification - both qualitatively and quantitatively. The quantitative assessment was conducted under two distinct conditions. When the latent representation was fed into a state-of-the-art splice site classifier, it demonstrated significant improvements, exceeding 80%. Moreover, it was observed that the latent representation maintains crucial information regarding splice sites and genomic context, thereby aiding in the understanding of DNA coding mechanisms.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates considering the effects of surface modification. Utilizing low-energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, this study examines how the surface termination of V$_2$O$_3$ films impacts its electronic structure. Our findings indicate that films grown on an Al$_2$O$_3$ substrate and left to anneal in ultrahigh vacuum exhibit a sub surface reduction that varies depending on the specific surface orientation, while those exposed to oxygen reveal fully oxidized surfaces across all crystallographic orientations. It's demonstrated that the oxidation process recovers the charge gap seen in previous studies but doesn't alter the quasiparticle band positions, providing further insight into the nature of the insulating state, which is attributed to the absence of 3d band states. Our results suggest that screening between layers limits the metal-insulator transition by increasing the energy of conduction by as much as two orders of magnitude. Finally, it's seen that low-energy electron doping fails to transform the V$_2$O$_3$ insulating state due to the absence of 3d band states, but raises the V 3p derived band just below the Fermi level, creating a pseudo-gap, and creates a large energy range, roughly spanning from 0.5 eV to the Mott-Ioffe

A new, systematic approach has been developed to construct smooth solutions for Lie-Poisson systems through a dual momentum map technique. This approach establishes a direct relationship between Lie-Poisson systems and Hamiltonian systems on cotangent bundles, leveraging a novel Poisson bracket definition. By doing so, it allows for a natural extension of symplectic integrators to solve Lie-Poisson systems. This approach can further generalize results obtained by Ferguson, Lu and Wang, and it provides a new insight into existing results obtained by other researchers, including one of the authors. Furthermore, it lays the foundation for a dual momentum map technique in the context of continuous Lie-Poisson systems.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder in 2018, resulting in 9 newly identified and 8 previously known planets in the sub-prime field.
